title: Basis of preparation
heading: 7.1.1 Basis of preparation
start_phrase: This disclosure is prepared based on the Sustainability statements in our Integrated Annual Report 2024.
summary:
- Purpose and scope: Qualitative information on ESG risk (Tables 1–3), with disclosures based on the Sustainability Statements in the Integrated Annual Report 2024. The double materiality assessment (DMA) underpins the disclosures.
- Materiality approach: Multiple, interconnected assessments—Integrated Reporting (IR), European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), and ECB climate-related and environmental risks (CER) integrated into the Enterprise Risk Management framework. In 2024, the ECB CER assessment was integrated into the ESRS assessment. Enhancements include updated Environmental and Social Heatmaps, the CASY client assessment tool, and a strengthened risk appetite framework. 2024 CER results inform the DMA as financial materiality input.
- Time horizons: Short term (1 year), medium term (1–5 years), and long term (>5 years), with deviations disclosed per topic. Emphasis on forward-looking reporting for sustainability matters.
- Scenario analysis: Assessment based on a global base case where economies pursue decarbonisation but fall short of the Paris <2°C goal, implying ~2.2°C warming by 2100. The scenario sits between IEA Announced Pledges and Stated Policies, includes chronic physical shocks, and aligns with assumptions used in IFRS financial statements.
- Critical assumptions: Physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts) can reduce business productivity and damage property; in the short term, transition risks increase costs for companies adapting to a low‑carbon economy.
text:
Basis of preparation
This disclosure is prepared based on the Sustainability statements in our Integrated Annual Report 2024. Results of our  
double materiality assessment (DMA) constitutes the backbone of the disclosures.

title: Our materiality assessment
heading: 7.1.2 Our materiality assessment
start_phrase: We conduct multiple materiality assessments, each serving distinct yet interconnected purposes.
summary:
- Focus: Qualitative information on ESG risk (Tables 1–3) and the basis of preparation drawn from ABN AMRO’s Integrated Annual Report 2024, with the double materiality assessment (DMA) as the backbone.
- Materiality approach: Multiple, interconnected assessments—Integrated Reporting (IR), European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), and ECB climate-related and environmental risks (CER) within the ERM framework. In 2024, the ECB CER assessment was integrated into ESRS. Enhancements include Environmental and Social Heatmaps, the CASY client assessment tool, and updates to the risk appetite framework. CER results inform the financial materiality leg of the DMA.
- Time horizons: Short term (1 year), medium term (1–5 years), and long term (>5 years), with deviations disclosed per topic.
- Scenario analysis: A global base case with partial decarbonisation, not fully Paris-aligned; compatible with ~2.2°C warming by 2100, between IEA Announced Pledges and Stated Policies scenarios. Includes chronic physical risk damages. IFRS financial statement assumptions are aligned to this scenario.
- Critical assumptions: Physical risks (e.g., floods, drought) may reduce business productivity and damage property; transition risks are expected to increase short-term costs for companies, with additional transition effects implied (text truncated).
text:
Our materiality assessment
We conduct multiple materiality assessments, each serving distinct yet interconnected purposes. These include:
•the Integrated Reporting (IR) materiality assessment,
•the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) materiality assessment,
•the European Central Bank (ECB) climate-related and environmental risks (CER) materiality assessment as 
integrated in the Enterprise Risk Management framework.
Each of these assessments has its own specific methodology, which we explain in detail below. This year, the ECB 
Guide CER materiality assessment has been integrated into the ESRS materiality assessment. To advance our ESG risk 
management practices and comply with the expectations of the ECB Guide on CER we made many improvements in 
2024, for example in the Environmental and Social Heatmaps , the CASY tool for client assessment  and the risk 
appetite framework . 
The 2024 CER materiality assessment results fed into the double materiality assessment as financial materiality input.

title: Time horizons
heading: 7.1.3 Time horizons
start_phrase: We assess material impacts, risks and opportunities over the short, medium and long term.
summary:
- Scope and basis: Qualitative ESG risk disclosures for Tables 1–3, prepared from the Sustainability Statements in the Integrated Annual Report 2024, with the double materiality assessment (DMA) as the backbone.
- Materiality approach: Multiple, interconnected assessments—Integrated Reporting (IR), ESRS, and ECB climate-related and environmental risks (CER) within the Enterprise Risk Management framework. In 2024, the ECB CER assessment was integrated into the ESRS assessment.
- 2024 enhancements: Strengthened ESG risk management via updated Environmental and Social Heatmaps, the CASY client assessment tool, and refinements to the risk appetite framework.
- Linkages: 2024 CER materiality results were used as financial materiality input to the DMA.
- Time horizons: Short term = 1 year, medium term = 1–5 years, long term = >5 years; deviations are disclosed per topic.
- Scenario basis: Global base case assumes broad but insufficient decarbonisation to meet <2°C, with a mid-point of ~2.2°C warming; positioned between IEA Announced Pledges and Stated Policies scenarios; includes chronic physical shocks; IFRS assumptions aligned to this scenario.
- Critical assumptions: Physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts) can reduce business productivity and damage property; in the short term, transition risks increase companies’ costs as they move toward a low-carbon economy. The text truncates before completing further transition risk details.
text:
Time horizons
We assess material impacts, risks and opportunities over the short, medium and long term. The short term refers to the 
reporting period of the Annual Financial Statements. Since sustainability-related matters often materialise over longer 
time horizons, the nature of these topics warrants more forward-looking reporting, whereas financial information is 
related to the annual reporting period. For forward-looking information on ABN AMRO’s material impacts, risks and 
opportunities in the Sustainability Statements, ABN AMRO defines:
• 1 year as short term
• between 1 and 5 years as medium term
• more than 5 years as long term
Where our time horizons deviate from these general guiding principles, this is disclosed alongside the specific material 
topic.

title: Scenarios
heading: 7.1.4 Scenarios
start_phrase: The assessment was performed against our global base case scenario, in which a large group of countries make systems changes with a view to decarbonising their economies through policy reform and other initiatives.
summary:
- Scope and basis: Qualitative ESG risk disclosures for Tables 1–3, prepared from the Sustainability Statements in the Integrated Annual Report 2024, with the double materiality assessment (DMA) as the backbone.
- Materiality approach: Multiple, interlinked assessments—Integrated Reporting (IR), ESRS, and ECB climate-related and environmental risks (CER) embedded in Enterprise Risk Management. In 2024, the ECB CER assessment was integrated into the ESRS assessment.
- 2024 enhancements: Advancements to meet ECB Guide on CER expectations, including updated Environmental and Social Heatmaps, the CASY client assessment tool, and an enhanced risk appetite framework.
- Integration of results: 2024 CER materiality outcomes feed into the DMA as financial materiality input.
- Time horizons: Short term = 1 year; medium term = 1–5 years; long term = >5 years, with any deviations disclosed per topic.
- Scenario context: A global base case with ongoing decarbonisation that falls short of the Paris <2°C goal, implying ~2.2°C warming by 2100; positioned between IEA Announced Pledges and Stated Policies scenarios; includes chronic physical shocks; IFRS assumptions aligned to this scenario.
- Critical assumptions: Physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts) can reduce business productivity and damage property; near-term transition risks increase company costs as they move toward a low-carbon model; further transition impacts are implied but text is truncated.
text:
Scenarios
The assessment was performed against our global base case scenario, in which a large group of countries make 
systems changes with a view to decarbonising their economies through policy reform and other initiatives.  However, 
the overall reduction in GHG emissions is falling short of meeting the Paris target of reigning in average global 
warming to less than 2°C from pre-industrial levels by 2100. Instead, our baseline scenario is compatible with global 
warming with a mid-point of approximately 2.2°C. This scenario for global emissions falls somewhere between the 
IEA’s Announced Pledges Scenario and the Stated Policies scenario. The scenario also embeds damage caused by 
chronic physical shocks. The assumptions used in preparing our IFRS financial statements are aligned with this 
scenario.

title: Critical assumptions
heading: 7.1.5 Critical assumptions
start_phrase: To assess the financial impact of CER risks, we assumed that physical risk, such as floods or drought, may lead to loss of productivity for businesses and property damage for home owners.
summary:
- Scope: Qualitative ESG risk disclosures (Tables 1–3), prepared from the Sustainability Statements in the Integrated Annual Report 2024, with the double materiality assessment (DMA) as the backbone.
- Materiality: Multiple, interconnected assessments—Integrated Reporting (IR), ESRS, and ECB climate-related and environmental risks (CER)—with the ECB CER assessment integrated into the ESRS DMA in 2024. Enhancements include Environmental and Social Heatmaps, the CASY client assessment tool, and updates to the risk appetite framework. CER results feed into the DMA as financial materiality input.
- Time horizons: Short term (1 year), medium term (1–5 years), long term (>5 years), with deviations disclosed per topic.
- Scenario basis: Global base case with partial decarbonisation progress consistent with ~2.2°C warming by 2100 (between IEA APS and STEPS), including chronic physical damage; IFRS financial statement assumptions aligned to this scenario.
- Critical assumptions: Physical risks (e.g., floods, droughts) may reduce business productivity and damage properties; transition risks raise costs, may render business models obsolete or shrink demand; properties with weaker energy labels may face price declines.
- Metrics and uncertainty: Reliance on estimates, averages, and assumptions; data sourced from clients and external vendors, with sector averages used when necessary; combined data for certain metrics (e.g., financed emissions). Lower accuracy than financial metrics, especially for value chain data, due to evolving reporting, limited historical data, and non-uniform measurement practices; commitment to transparency on data and assumption changes.
- Risk definition: Sustainability risk is the potential for ESG factors to cause negative financial or non-financial impacts on the bank or society, directly or via other risk types; it is a material risk integral to the bank’s risk profile and strategy.
- Transmission channels: Microeconomic (impacts on individual clients leading to financial risks for the bank) and macroeconomic (impacts on broader economic factors that adversely affect the bank).
text:
Critical assumptions
To assess the financial impact of CER risks, we assumed that physical risk, such as floods or drought, may lead to loss 
of productivity for businesses and property damage for home owners. In the short term, transition risk is expected to 
lead to higher costs for companies transitioning to a carbon-free environment. The transition may also result in some ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
194companies’ business models becoming obsolete or in a significant drop in demand. For home owners, transition risk 
may lead to a fall in the prices of properties with weaker energy labels.

title: Metrics and estimation uncertainty
heading: 7.1.6 Metrics and estimation uncertainty
start_phrase: In this report we use metrics, especially in the case of our client portfolios, that are based on certain estimates, averages or assumptions.
summary:
- Transition risks can render companies’ business models obsolete, reduce product demand, and depress housing values for properties with weaker energy labels.
- Reported sustainability metrics rely on estimates, averages, assumptions, and multiple data sources (client-reported data, external vendors, sector averages), with financed emissions combining several sources.
- The accuracy of these sustainability metrics is generally lower than for financial metrics; quality varies by whether data is directly reported or proxy-based, externally reviewed, forward-looking vs. historical, and whether established frameworks exist.
- Value chain-related quantitative metrics carry high measurement uncertainty due to immature sustainability reporting among counterparties.
- Data quality and comparability are expected to improve over time as regulation standardizes disclosures, but current comparability is limited by scarce historical data and non-uniform measurement practices; different acceptable methodologies may be applied initially.
- The bank commits to transparent disclosure of changes in data and assumptions to explain movements and provide context.
- Sustainability risk is defined as the potential negative financial or non-financial impact from ESG factors on the bank or society, directly or via other risk types; it is a material risk integral to ABN AMRO’s risk management and strategy.
- ESG factors act as drivers of traditional risk types, transmitted through:
  - Microeconomic channels affecting individual clients and thus the bank’s financial risk.
  - Macroeconomic channels affecting broader economic variables (e.g., productivity, growth) that in turn impact the bank.
text:
Metrics and estimation uncertainty
In this report we use metrics, especially in the case of our client portfolios, that are based on certain estimates, 
averages or assumptions. The underlying data either comes directly from clients or is sourced from external data 
vendors. We use sector averages if we cannot reasonably collect information, especially from our value chain business 
relationships. For certain metrics, such as our financed emissions, we combine several data sources. 
Generally, the level of accuracy of these metrics is lower than that of financial metrics, given the quality of the inputs. 
The quality typically depends on whether the data is directly reported by our clients or based on proxies, the 
characteristics of that reported data and whether it has been reviewed by an external party, whether the data is 
forward-looking or historical and whether established measurement frameworks are available.  All quantitative metrics 
relating to information on our value chain currently have a high measurement uncertainty as sustainability reporting is 
a developing field for most actors in our value chain and we depend on these actors for accurate informatio n.
The data we use is subject to continuous improvement, given also that sustainability-related regulation may result in 
more standardised data becoming available in the future. Comparability of sustainability information between entities 
and over time may be affected by the lack of historical sustainability information  and by the absence of uniform 
practices for evaluating and measuring this information. This allows for the application of different, but acceptable, 
measurement techniques, especially in the initial years. We aim to be transparent in our disclosures on any changes in 
underlying data or assumptions in order to explain movements and provide the appropriate context to readers of the 
report.

title: Background and definitions of sustainability risk
heading: 7.1.7 Background and definitions of sustainability risk
start_phrase: Sustainability risk is defined in our risk taxonomy and sustainability risk policy as the risk that Environmental, Social or Governance-related (ESG) factors have a negative financial and/or non-financial impact on ABN AMRO or the wider society, either directly or via other risk types.
summary:
- Highlights transition risks that can render companies’ business models obsolete or depress demand, and notes potential declines in home prices for properties with weaker energy labels.
- Explains that sustainability metrics used (e.g., financed emissions) rely on estimates, averages, assumptions, and multiple data sources (client-reported data, external vendors, sector averages), leading to lower accuracy than financial metrics.
- Stresses high measurement uncertainty for value-chain data due to evolving sustainability reporting, varied data quality (direct vs proxy, reviewed vs unreviewed, forward-looking vs historical), and uneven availability of established measurement frameworks.
- Notes that data quality and comparability should improve over time with regulation and standardisation, but initial years may involve different acceptable measurement techniques; commits to transparent disclosure of data or assumption changes.
- Defines sustainability risk as ESG-related factors that can negatively affect ABN AMRO or society, directly or via traditional risk types; managing it is material to the bank’s risk profile and strategy.
- Describes transmission channels for sustainability risk:
  - Microeconomic: impacts on individual clients that translate into financial risks for the bank.
  - Macroeconomic: impacts on broader economic variables (e.g., productivity, growth) that in turn affect the bank.
- Outlines strategic focus on where impacts occur in the value chain:
  - Main downstream impact is through financed clients in lending portfolios (mortgages, corporate loans); consumer loan relevance depends on use of proceeds per EU Taxonomy.
  - Non-lending activities may be impactful but accounting methodologies are evolving; financed emissions methods for government bonds and underwriting exist, though broader guidance and approaches for undrawn facilities and guarantees remain unclear.
- States that client assets (investments managed or facilitated) are considered relevant for sustainability; influence varies by service model (discretionary, advisory, execution-only); discloses climate mitigation and workers-in-the-value-chain information.
- Acknowledges additional positive and negative impacts via products, services, and strategic choices (e.g., privacy, financial inclusion, access to services), with more detail in the Social section of the Integrated Annual Report.
- Describes a two-pronged ESG risk assessment:
  - Inside-out risks: clients’ impacts on people/planet that can create financial and non-financial risks for the bank (e.g., pollution cleanup costs).
  - Outside-in risks: climate and environmental factors affecting the bank and its clients, split into:
    - Transition risks (policy, regulation, consumer preferences, technology shifts).
    - Physical risks (acute events like floods; chronic trends like rising temperatures and biodiversity loss), with examples such as flooding affecting mortgage collateral values.
text:
Background  and definitions of sustainability risk
Sustainability risk is defined in our risk taxonomy and sustainability risk policy as the risk that Environmental, Social or 
Governance-related (ESG) factors have a negative financial and/or non-financial impact on ABN AMRO or the wider 
society, either directly or via other risk types. As sustainability risk is considered a material risk in our risk taxonomy, 
managing sustainability risk is a fundamental part of safeguarding our risk profile and supporting ABN AMRO’s 
strategic objectives. 
ESG factors can create increased risks for the bank. These, in turn, can adversely affect the bank’s financial and/or non-
financial performance and are a causal factor, or risk driver, of traditional risk types. 
Transmission channels are the causal pathways that explain how sustainability factors lead to increased financial and 
non-financial risks for the bank. Understanding transmission channels is therefore key to setting adequate measures to 
manage sustainability risk. Transmission channels can be classified as microeconomic or macroeconomic:
•Microeconomic transmission channels are causal chains by which sustainability risk affects the bank’s individual 
clients, resulting in financial risks for ABN AMRO.
•Macroeconomic transmission channels are causal chains by which sustainability risk affects macroeconomic factors 
(e.g. labour productivity or economic growth), which in in turn adversely affect ABN AMRO.ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡

title: Sustainability in relation to our strategy and business model
heading: 7.2.1 Sustainability in relation to our strategy and business model
start_phrase: The main impact in our value chain is the downstream impact associated with the clients we finance, primarily through our lending portfolios — such as mortgages and corporate loans — which are central to these Sustainability Statements.
summary:
- Explains ABN AMRO’s two-pronged approach to sustainability risk: inside-out risks (impacts clients may have on people and planet that can lead to financial and non-financial risk for the bank) and outside-in risks (how climate and environmental factors affect the bank and clients), with outside-in split into transition risk (policy, market, technology shifts) and physical risk (acute and chronic climate/environmental impacts).
- Identifies the bank’s main sustainability impacts as downstream, primarily via financed clients in lending portfolios (notably residential mortgages and corporate loans), with consumer loan relevance depending on use of proceeds aligned to EU Taxonomy.
- Notes evolving methodologies for non-lending activities: financed emissions for government bonds and underwriting exist but broader guidelines remain unclear; impacts of undrawn facilities and guarantees lack established assessment methods.
- Clarifies treatment of client assets (DPM, Advisory, Execution-only): influence varies by service, but they remain relevant for sustainability; the bank continues to disclose on climate mitigation and labor conditions in value chains.
- Links sustainability to the business model and asset mix, highlighting loans and advances as the core of total assets, predominantly mortgages and corporate loans, which drive the bank’s sustainability exposure and impact.
- Positions sustainability as a strategic pillar since 2018, operationalized via the Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS) since 2020; SAS measures “sustainability acceleration assets” bank-wide and by client unit, complements but does not replace ESRS metrics, and includes EU Taxonomy-aligned assets via the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- Differentiates between volume-based SAS/GAR and impact-based climate targets (GHG reductions), acknowledging that increases in SAS may not always directly translate to immediate emission reductions; commits to improving connectivity and clarity between KPIs and impacts.
- Confirms material topics and focus areas (climate, nature, social impact) through the bank’s Double Materiality Assessment (DMA); 2024 results required no strategic changes.
- Describes governance and planning: integration of material matters into strategy and financial planning, including initiatives, risks, and opportunities; recognition that climate and environmental risks are highly likely to materialize over the medium to long term, supported by bank-wide ICAAP stress testing.
- References broader social considerations (privacy, financial inclusion, access to services) addressed in the Integrated Annual Report’s Social section.
text:
Sustainability in relation to our strategy and business model
The main impact in our value chain is the downstream impact associated with the clients we finance, primarily through 
our lending portfolios — such as mortgages and corporate loans — which are central to these Sustainability 
Statements. The relevance of consumer loans depends on their use of proceeds, when known, in line with the 
principles of the EU Taxonomy Regulation. Examples are real estate, building renovation loans and motor vehicle 
loans. While our non-lending activities may have a significant environmental impact, best practices for accounting for 
them are still evolving. For instance, methodologies for calculating financed GHG emissions for government bonds 
and underwriting now exist, but broader guidelines for government exposures and underwriting remain unclear. 
Similarly, undrawn facilities and guarantees, although not on our balance sheet, facilitate economic activity, yet there 
is no established approach for assessing their impact. 
The influence ABN AMRO has on client assets (investments managed or facilitated for clients) varies depending on the 
service provided: Discretionary Portfolio Management, Advisory or Execution-only. Nevertheless, ABN AMRO regards 
client assets as relevant from a sustainability perspective, as evidenced by our previous reporting. In line with past 
years, we have again chosen to disclose information about our client assets portfolio with regard to climate change 
mitigation and workers in the value chain.
Besides the impacts identified through our downstream activities and based mainly on our lending portfolios, positive 
and negative impacts also occur through the products and services that we offer and through the strategic choices 
that are made regarding, for example, privacy, financial inclusion and access to services.  This is described in more 
detail in the Social section of the Integrated Annual Report 2024.ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
196
As part of overseeing ESG risks arising through its clients, 
ABN AMRO carries out a two-pronged assessment, 
whereby the bank manages the effects that our activities 
have on the world and society (inside-out) and also on 
how sustainability matters may affect us through the 
physical and transition risks we are exposed to (outside-
in). More specifically:
•‘Inside-out risks’ are the financial and non-financial 
risks arising when clients of the bank may have an 
effect on people or the planet through ESG factors 
(which is also defined as impact within ABN AMRO). 
This impact can be direct; for example, if a client 
causes and has to clean up water pollution.
•‘Outside-in risks’ are the financial and non-financial 
risks arising when climate or environmental factors 
may have an effect on the bank and its clients (either 
at an individual client or portfolio level). For example, 
extreme weather events such as flooding can have an 
effect on the value of a client’s collateral in the bank’s 
mortgage portfolio. Outside-in risks are, in turn, split 
into transition risks and physical risks:
◦ Transition risk refers to financial and non-
financial risks that result, directly or indirectly, from the 
process of adjusting to a lower-carbon and more 
environmentally sustainable economy (e.g. changes in 
regulation, consumer preferences or technology).
◦ Physical risk refers to the financial risk of climate 
change and environmental degradation. Physical risk can 
be acute (for example, when it relates to extreme 
weather events) or chronic (when it relates to progressive 
shifts such as rising temperatures and biodiversity loss). Linking our business model to sustainability matters

title: Sustainability as part of our strategy
heading: 7.2.2 Sustainability as part of our strategy
start_phrase: Sustainability is a key component of ABN AMRO’s strategy, representing one of three strategic pillars.
summary:
- The document links ABN AMRO’s business model and balance sheet to sustainability, indicating which components relate, partly relate, or do not relate to sustainability matters.
- Balance sheet snapshot: total assets split into Loans and advances (65%), Financial investments (12%), and Other assets (23%); within Loans and advances, Residential mortgages (61%), Corporate loans (33%), Consumer loans (3%), and Other (3%).
- Sustainability is one of three strategic pillars, embedded since 2018 and operationalised via ambitions and targets since 2020 (ahead of CSRD).
- The Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS) is used to steer and set accountability across the bank and client units; it measures “sustainability (acceleration) assets” and includes topics deemed material in the DMA (e.g., climate change, circular economy).
- SAS is a volume-based KPI, includes EU Taxonomy-aligned assets via the Green Asset Ratio (GAR), and is designed to enable and stimulate client transition; it is not an ESRS metric nor a direct measure of progress on specific material matters.
- Complementary climate strategy metrics focus on direct impact through GHG emissions reductions; SAS growth can support climate pathways when directed to relevant sectors and mitigation purposes, but links can be indirect or time-lagged.
- Priority is to ensure KPIs are clearly tied to intended impacts and to improve connectivity across different sustainability metrics and targets while retaining metric diversity for different purposes.
- The bank’s material matters (from the DMA) are integrated into three focus areas: climate, nature, and social impact; 2024 DMA results confirmed no new or diminished material matters, so no immediate strategic changes are required.
- The financial plan outlines ongoing initiatives and associated risks and opportunities tied to these material topics.
- Climate-related and environmental risks are assessed as highly likely to materialise over the medium to long term; a bank-wide ICAAP stress test evaluated the financial impact of environmental and other risks.
text:
Sustainability as part of our strategy
Sustainability is a key component of ABN AMRO’s strategy, representing one of three strategic pillars. Sustainability 
has been part of our strategy since 2018, and has been operationalised through our sustainability ambitions and 
targets since 2020, ahead of CSRD.
In line with the role of sustainability as a pillar, we have steered on and set accountability via our Sustainability 
Acceleration Standard (SAS). The SAS itself is a comprehensive methodology for measuring our Sustainability 
(acceleration) assets so as to assess our performance bank-wide and on a client-unit level.
SAS, as an overarching metric, includes topics defined as material in our DMA assessment (such as climate change and 
circular economy), but was not developed for the purpose of measuring the progress of the identified material matters 
and should not be considered a metric under ESRS. The value of SAS as a KPI is that it aims to enable and stimulate 
clients (and bankers) in their transition to become more sustainable.
ABN AMRO does not solely steer its sustainability efforts on SAS. We have also set climate targets to reduce our 
impact on climate, and are working to identify impact-related metrics for other material matters. 
SAS, including EU taxonomy-aligned assets measured by the Green Asset Ratio (GAR), is a volume-based metric, while 
the climate strategy metrics have a direct impact (on GHG emission reductions). In several cases, a positive 
development in SAS volume will have a positive impact on our pathway towards climate targets, if these loans are 
provided to clients in sectors in scope and the loan is aimed at mitigating climate impact. However, not all cases have 
a direct link between SAS (or GAR) and climate reduction pathways as, in some cases, loans will only have an impact 
on client emissions at a later moment in time. 
Our first priority in this context is ensuring that KPIs and metrics are clearly linked to the impacts they aim to measure. 
In the future, we aim to further enhance the connectivity between different sustainability metrics and targets, 
recognising that different metrics may still be needed for different purposes.

title: Current and anticipated effects of material matters on strategy and business model
heading: 7.2.3 Current and anticipated effects of material matters on strategy and business model
start_phrase: ABN AMRO’s strategy incorporates the material matters identified in the DMA through three focus areas: climate, nature and social impact.
summary:
- The document links ABN AMRO’s business model to sustainability matters and maps business components to their sustainability relevance.
- Portfolio context: approximately 65% of total assets are loans and advances, 12% financial investments, and 23% other assets. Within the loan book, about 61% are residential mortgages, 33% corporate loans, 3% consumer loans, and 3% other.
- Sustainability is one of three strategic pillars since 2018 and has been operationalised with ambitions and targets since 2020 (ahead of CSRD).
- The Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS) is the bank’s overarching methodology to measure “sustainability (acceleration) assets” at bank and client-unit level. It incorporates DMA-identified topics (e.g., climate change, circular economy) but is not an ESRS metric; its purpose is to stimulate client transition.
- SAS (including EU Taxonomy-aligned assets via the Green Asset Ratio, GAR) is volume-based, while climate strategy metrics target direct GHG reductions. SAS growth can support climate targets but not all SAS/GAR activities have immediate or direct emission impacts. The bank aims to further connect different sustainability KPIs while keeping them purpose-fit.
- Material matters and strategy: DMA confirms three focus areas—climate, nature, and social impact—with no changes in 2024. The business model remains resilient; an ICAAP stress test over five years shows climate and environmental risks are within loss-absorbing capacity.
- Client transition approach: ABN AMRO prioritises stimulating and supporting client decarbonisation and sustainability (e.g., mortgage incentives for sustainable home improvements), while balancing environmental and social considerations and avoiding lending discrimination based on physical risk indicators.
- Environmental impacts arise mainly through financed activities (clients), covering climate change, air and water pollution, biodiversity loss, and circular economy challenges; the bank’s own operational footprint is small. ABN AMRO aims to be clients’ first-choice sustainability partner through financing and expertise.
- Social impact: focus on equality and human rights across operations and client relationships; initiatives to foster inclusivity and resilience target diverse groups (women, minorities, people with disabilities, refugees, generations, LGBTIQ+, neurodiversity), including programmes such as Reboot and B-able.
- Opportunities: the energy transition presents significant growth potential; ABN AMRO plans up to EUR 1 billion in early-stage capital by 2030 (direct equity, fund investments, hybrid debt) and aims to increase lending to renewable energy and decarbonisation technologies to EUR 10 billion by 2030.
text:
Current and anticipated effects of material matters on strategy and business model
ABN AMRO’s strategy incorporates the material matters identified in the DMA through three focus areas: climate, 
nature and social impact. Since no new material matters were identified, and no previously identified matters lost their 
relevance, the 2024 outcomes confirmed the relevance of our current focus areas, requiring no immediate 
adjustments to our approach. In the following sections we explain how each material topic impacts ABN AMRO and 
outline the bank’s actions in response. The financial plan also details existing initiatives, alongside associated risks 
and opportunities. 
As part of the DMA, the bank determined that climate-related and environmental risks are highly likely to materialise 
over the medium to long term. A bank-wide ICAAP stress test evaluated the financial impact of ER and other risks over ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
197a five-year horizon, concluding that the effects are well within our loss-absorbing capacity. This confirms the business 
model is sufficiently resilient to cover the risks in our adverse scenario. As a result, we consider the design of our 
business model resilient to these risks.  For more details, refer to the Business risk  section in the Risk, capital and 
funding chapter of the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
ABN AMRO’s approach to addressing climate and environmental risks centres on stimulating and supporting clients’ 
transition efforts. For example, we offer financial incentives within residential mortgage te rms to encourage 
sustainable home improvements. At the same time, we need to balance material matters such as the environmental 
and social aspects of sustainability. For example, we acknowledge our social duty as an enabler of home ownership. 
Consequently, we do not discriminate in lending based on physical risk indicators. Our assessment and approach 
remain consistent with the previous year.

title: Climate and environmental effects
heading: 7.2.4.1 Climate and environmental effects
start_phrase: ABN AMRO primarily impacts the environment through its clients.

- Business model resilience: Stress testing over a five-year adverse scenario shows impacts are within loss-absorbing capacity, confirming the model’s resilience; approach consistent with prior year.

Implements inclusivity initiatives for diverse groups (women, minorities, people with disabilities, refugees, generations, LGBTIQ+, neurodiversity) including Reboot and B-able programmes.

text:
Climate and environmental effects
ABN AMRO primarily impacts the environment through its clients. These impacts include climate change, air and water 
pollution, biodiversity loss and challenges related to the circular economy, each of which can have cascading effects. 
Most environmental effects arise from the financing, investment products and other services we provide, while our 
own operations have a very small environmental footprint. As we finance a diverse range of economic activities, 
describing the effect, or potential effect, of material matters on people and the environment in a comprehensive way 
is challenging. For example, climate change may lead to short-term economic costs through more frequent and 
severe extreme weather events. These economic costs can further increase in the long term due to persistent climate 
change impacts, including further temperature rise, glacial and ice sheet melting and ocean acidification. Air pollution 
can harm ecosystems, contribute to respiratory and chronic diseases and reduce agricultural yields.
ABN AMRO strives to be its clients’ first-choice partner in sustainability by offering financing and expertise to support 
their transition to more sustainable business models. We also align our operations and client engagement with climate 
and environmental objectives.

text:
Social effects
The bank’s approach to social impact aims to foster equality and protect human rights. We address social impacts 
both within our operations and through our clients’ activities. ABN AMRO recognises the positive and negative effects 
of social impacts; for example, equal treatment and opportunities for all can have positive effects such as improved 
team dynamics, but also negative effects such as mental health strains if treatment is perceived as unequal. 
ABN AMRO has launched various initiatives to enhance workplace inclusivity and contribute to broader societal goals. 
We integrate social considerations into our operations to create a more inclusive and resilient bank. These efforts 
include initiatives targeting diverse groups, such as women, individuals from minority cultural or ethnic backgrounds, 
people with disabilities, asylum seekers with refugee status, different generations and the LGBTIQ+ community. 
Activities focusing, for example, on neurodiversity and our Reboot and B-able programmes reflect our objectives 
in these respects.  More details can be found in the Social section of the Sustainability statements chapter in Integrated 
Annual Report 2024.

title: Sustainability risk governance relating to ABN AMRO’s clients
heading: 7.3.2 Sustainability risk governance relating to ABN AMRO’s clients
start_phrase: Risk management sub-committees (positioned directly below the Board-level executive committees) support effective and efficient risk management throughout the bank, each with their own remit:
summary:
- ABN AMRO applies a Sustainability Risk Management Framework aligned with its enterprise risk management (ERM) cycle to manage sustainability risks, including negative impacts, related to clients across their full lifecycle (onboarding, ongoing due diligence, potential exit).
- The framework operationalises risk governance and the Sustainability Risk Policy Framework for downstream value chain risks and is supported by tools such as climate/environmental/social risk heatmaps, materiality assessments, portfolio scenario analysis, CASY (Client Assessment on SustainabilitY), stress testing, lending criteria, engagement, risk appetite setting, and sustainability risk reporting to business, risk and executive committees.
- Governance is executed through risk sub-committees beneath Board-level executive committees:
  - Business Risk Committees (oversight of sustainability risk in client units; approve unit-specific issues; monthly/quarterly).
  - Scenario and Stress-test Committee (oversight of climate/environmental risks, scenarios and stress tests; quarterly).
  - Financial Crime Risk Committee (bank-wide decisions on financial crime risks, including sustainability aspects like proceeds of environmental crime; monthly).
  - Methodology Acceptance Group (validates risk and climate stress testing models; monthly).
  - Impairment & Provisioning Committee (manages impairments/provisions, including climate transition-related credit losses; monthly).
- Day-to-day oversight is performed by the Sustainability Risk team within Central Risk Management. The first-line Engagement Committee oversees client, sector and material supplier engagements on ESG risk, ensuring documentation and alignment with bank policies, the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and OECD Guidelines.
- The Sustainability Risk Policy Framework comprises the Sustainability Risk Policy, Standards and Exclusions, reviewed annually to reflect new insights, stakeholder views and regulatory guidance (ECB/EBA). Exclusions include an Exclusion List and a Controversial Weapons List.
- Standards referenced include the Sustainability Acceleration Standard, Sustainability Risk Standard for Defence, Sustainability Risk Standard for Project Finance, and a Sustainability Risk Standard with Client Requirements, supported by a Risk Taxonomy.
- The Sustainability Risk Policy sets principles and minimum requirements for managing client-related sustainability risks, covering definitions, governance, engagement with non-compliant clients, and controls across client onboarding, lifecycle management, lending and proprietary investments. It is approved by the Group Risk Committee under delegated authority from the Executive Board, reviewed at least annually with internal and external stakeholder input, and communicated across the first and second lines of defence, with a public abbreviated version available.
text:
Risk management sub-committees (positioned directly below the Board-level executive committees) support effective 
and efficient risk management throughout the bank, each with their own remit: 
•Business Risk Committees (BRCs) for oversight on sustainability risk within the specific client units and approval of 
client unit-specific sustainability risk issues (e.g. scenario analysis). The BRCs meet monthly or quarterly.
•Scenario and Stress-test Committee (SSC) for oversight on climate-related and environmental risks, scenario 
analyses and stress testing. The SSC meets quarterly.
•Financial Crime Risk Committee (FCRC) approves bank-wide and client unit-overarching decisions on financial 
crime risks related to money laundering, financing of terrorism, sanctions, bribery, corruption, tax integrity and fraud 
within the client lifecycle. As part of its remit, the FCRC may deal with sustainability-related aspects in relation, for 
example, to proceeds of environmental crime. The FCRC meets monthly.
•Methodology Acceptance Group (MAG) approves decisions on the validation and subsequent use of risk models 
and other models, for example climate stress testing methodologies and models. The MAG meets monthly.
•Impairment & Provisioning Committee (IPC), which designs, implements and manages enterprise-wide 
impairments, provisions and value adjustment programmes. As part of its remit, the IPC may deal with 
sustainability-related aspects in relation, for example, to credit losses that may arise in the context of climate 
transition risk. The IPC meets monthly.
Alongside these risk committees, day-to-day activities and oversight are performed by the Sustainability Risk team 
within Central Risk Management. 
The above risk sub-committees are supported by other first-line-of-defence committees such as the Engagement 
Committee, which is one of the executive business-led committees. The Engagement Committee is mandated by the 
Executive Board and is responsible for overseeing the bank’s engagement activities regarding clients, sectors and ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
199material suppliers so as to ensure that material ESG risk engagement is appropriately documented and that adequate 
measures are taken to stay within the bank’s chosen ESG risk. The aim of such engagement approach is to operate in 
compliance with the bank’s policies for the management of ESG risks, as well as with the UN Guiding Principles on 
Business and Human Rights (UNGPs) and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises.

text:
Sustainability risk policy framework
Our Sustainability Risk Policy Framework underpins how the bank manages sustainability risk, including negative 
impacts, in relation to our clients. The Sustainability Risk Policy Framework includes our sustainability risk policy, as 
well as standards and exclusions. It is subject to an annual review to incorporate new insights and practices, internal 
and external developments, and views of stakeholders, as well as to align with the latest regulatory guidance, such as 
ECB and EBA requirements and definitions.
The exclusions applied by ABN AMRO relate to specific activities outlined in the Governance of sustainability matters  
section of the Integrated Annual Report 2024. In practice, these exclusions mean that we will not knowingly provide 
financial products or services on our Exclusion List, or engage in business with a client listed in our Controversial 
Weapons List.

title: Sustainability-related standards and generic principles applicable to corporate clients
heading: 7.3.4 Sustainability-related standards and generic principles applicable to corporate clients
start_phrase: Our Standards and Generic Principles define the sustainability requirements against which our corporate clients must be assessed to ensure appropriate risk response measures.
summary:
The excerpt outlines a bank’s sustainability-related standards and generic principles that underpin its Sustainability Risk Policy Framework (SRPF) for assessing corporate clients, especially in higher-risk sectors. Core client expectations include legal compliance and transparency; identification and mitigation of salient human rights risks; a satisfactory ESG track record; meaningful stakeholder engagement and grievance handling; promotion of circularity and reduced virgin material use; monitoring and reduction of GHG emissions in line with the Paris Agreement; awareness of and action to preserve ecosystem services; preparedness for the Net Zero transition; management of impacts on biodiversity, water, air, and soil; and mitigation of physical climate risks.

These Generic Principles are the foundation of ESG assessments for all corporate financing and are operationalised across Corporate Banking, Wealth Management, and Personal & Business Banking. They support alignment with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, and address EU Taxonomy Article 18. The underlying Standard with Client Requirements has been enhanced for consistent application across clients, aligned with CSRD/ESRS terminology, and calibrated to client maturity by size and sector. Sectoral updates include: (1) expanded exclusion of direct lending to oil and gas fields licensed for development after 2023, in line with the IEA Net Zero 2050 scenario; and (2) removal of the exclusion on stand-alone project finance for nuclear power, coupled with strengthened due diligence and stringent financing criteria. The text also situates these requirements within the bank’s Sustainability Risk Management Framework and ERM cycle, where strategy is set by the first line of defence and oversight is provided by the second line.
text:
Sustainability-related standards and generic principles applicable to corporate clients
Generic principles
Minimum sustainability requirements underpinning the SRPF (Sustainability Risk Policy Framework) for corporate clients 
operating in higher-risk sectors
Clients comply with applicable laws and regulations 
and are able to demonstrate transparency regarding 
their responsible business conduct.
Clients know the salient human rights risks of their own 
activities and business relationships and take measures 
to address these risks.
Clients have a satisfactory ESG track record.
Clients have identified potentially affected groups and 
other relevant stakeholders and engage with them 
constructively and openly in assessing and mitigating 
human rights risks and addressing any grievances.
Clients take measures to promote circularity and 
reduce the use of virgin material and waste (e.g. 
through design, recycling, life-time extension), if 
applicable.
Clients monitor their GHG emissions and take 
measures to reduce them in line with the Paris climate 
goals.
Clients are aware of how their business model 
depends on ecosystem services (i.e. resources, 
pollination) and take measures to preserve these 
services.
Clients are aware of what the transition to a Net Zero 
economy means for their business model and take 
appropriate measures to prepare for the transition.
Clients are aware of their impact on biodiversity, water, 
air and soil and take appropriate measures to prevent 
biodiversity loss and pollution.
Clients are aware of the physical risks of a changing 
climate for their business model and take appropriate 
measures to mitigate these risks.
Our Standards and Generic Principles define the sustainability requirements against which our corporate clients must 
be assessed to ensure appropriate risk response measures.
The Generic Principles form the foundation of our Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) assessment of the 
bank’s corporate clients to whom we provide corporate loans or other financing. These Generic Principles are 
operationalised into specific requirements for our Corporate Banking, Wealth Management, Personal & Business 
Banking clients. 
These Generic Principles support the assessment of whether our clients comply with the United Nations (UN) Guiding 
Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs) and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development 
(OECD) Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises (MNEs), where applicable and as required under Article 18 of the EU 
Taxonomy Regulation. Although our Generic Principles have remained the same, we have enhanced our underlying 
Standard with Client Requirements, so that it now applies consistently across all our clients, as well as aligning with 
the terminology used in the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and related European Sustainability 
Reporting Standards (ESRS). This Standard also considers the maturity of a client on its ESG journey by taking into 
account the size and/or sector in which the client is active. The Standard with Client Requirements has additionally 
been updated on two points relating to the energy sector: 
•Firstly, we have widened the lending exclusion to direct lending to oil and gas fields licensed for development to 
after 2023. This change aligns with the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) latest Net Zero Emissions (NZE) 2050 
scenario.
•Secondly, we have removed the exclusion of stand-alone project finance for nuclear power generation. This change 
is based on the recognition that nuclear power is an integral part of the global energy mix, as noted in the IEA NZE 
scenario, and is included in several countries’ transition strategies. However, given the inherent risks associated with 
nuclear power generation, we have reinforced our due diligence procedures and established stringent criteria for 
financing nuclear power projects.

title: Business strategy and strategic decision-making (steps 1 and 7)
heading: 7.3.5 Business strategy and strategic decision-making (steps 1 and 7)
start_phrase: The Sustainability Risk Management Framework, which operationalises how we manage sustainability matters via the ERM cycle, starts with the setting of the business strategy by the first line of defence.
summary:
- Outlines generic sustainability principles and minimum requirements for corporate clients, especially in higher-risk sectors, under the Sustainability Risk Policy Framework (SRPF).
- Client expectations include legal compliance, transparent responsible conduct, human rights due diligence and grievance handling, satisfactory ESG track record, stakeholder engagement, circularity and waste reduction, GHG monitoring and Paris-aligned reductions, safeguarding ecosystem services, preparation for Net Zero transition, protection of biodiversity, water, air and soil, and mitigation of physical climate risks.
- These principles form the foundation of ESG assessments across Corporate Banking, Wealth Management, and Personal & Business Banking, and support compliance with UNGPs, OECD MNE Guidelines, and EU Taxonomy Article 18.
- The Standard with Client Requirements has been enhanced to apply consistently across all clients, align with CSRD/ESRS terminology, and account for client maturity by size/sector.
- Energy sector policy updates: expanded exclusion of direct lending to oil and gas fields licensed for development after 2023 (aligned with IEA NZE 2050), and removal of the blanket exclusion for stand-alone project finance for nuclear power, paired with strengthened due diligence and strict financing criteria.
- Describes integration of sustainability into business strategy via the Sustainability Risk Management Framework and ERM cycle: first line sets strategy; second line provides risk oversight and control.
- Strategic decisions (client engagement, portfolio adjustments, climate strategy) are informed by sustainability risk insights; risk appetite limits reflect strategic sustainability commitments (e.g., carbon reduction), and KPIs/KRIs are considered together.
- Explains risk identification and materiality processes using Environmental and Social Risk heatmaps, quarterly emerging risk scans, and the Risk Event Register feeding the risk taxonomy and scenarios.
- Heatmaps assess sub-sectors’ inherent sensitivities across corporate lending and residential real estate, using sectoral (64 sub-sectors) and geographic lenses, and over 40 underlying physical, transition, and negative impact events.
- Aggregated heatmap scoring uses the most sensitive (conservative) factor among negative impact, transition risk, and physical risk to guide materiality, stress testing, and risk appetite.
text:
The Sustainability Risk Management Framework, which operationalises how we manage sustainability matters via the 
ERM cycle, starts with the setting of the business strategy by the first line of defence. The subsequent risk 
management monitoring and oversight are carried out by the second line of defence. ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
201The business strategy on sustainability matters cannot be set in isolation and, as such, has to align with the bank’s risk 
appetite and risk policies in the second line of defence. As a result, the business strategy and subsequent strategic 
decision-making go hand-in-hand with the risk control and oversight carried out in the ERM cycle (described in the 
next sections):  
•Insights into sustainability risks inform strategic decision-making. For example, the bank’s climate strategy   was 
developed partly in response to climate-related transition risks. Similarly, decisions to engage with a specific client 
or group of clients to accelerate the sustainability shift are informed by client- or sector-level risk identification and 
measurement, while decisions to reduce, maintain or expand certain portfolios are informed by our insights into 
sustainability risks.
•Sustainability risk management is also informed by ABN AMRO’s strategic commitments to sustainability matters. 
For example, our risk appetite limits take into account several elements, such as our strategic targets on carbon 
reduction. In other words, key performance indicators and key risk indicators should be looked at alongside each 
other. Similarly, the sustainability risk policy framework is updated regularly to assess, for example, clients’ 
alignment with our strategic objectives.

title: Risk identification and materiality assessment (step 2)
heading: 7.3.6 Risk identification and materiality assessment (step 2)
start_phrase: The risk identification part of the ERM cycle relies to a large extent on our Environmental and Social Risk heatmaps.
summary:
- The document describes how the bank’s sustainability strategy is integrated with its enterprise risk management (ERM) cycle and aligned with risk appetite and second line risk policies, creating a two-way linkage: sustainability risk insights guide strategic choices (client engagement, portfolio steering), while strategic commitments (e.g., carbon reduction targets) shape risk appetite limits and policy updates; KPIs and KRIs are considered together.
- Risk identification and materiality (ERM step 2) rely on Environmental & Social Risk heatmaps and quarterly emerging risk scans; the most material emerging risks feed the Risk Event Register, which informs the risk taxonomy and scenario booklet.
- The heatmaps assess inherent sensitivity to sustainability events across 64 corporate sub-sectors and relevant geographies in corporate lending (downstream value chain) and residential real estate, covering over 40 physical, transition, and negative impact events (e.g., flooding, water stress, policy/market effects, GHG emissions, water use intensity).
- Sensitivities are aggregated conservatively by taking the most sensitive factor per topic and presented across topics E1–E5 (climate change, pollution, water/marine resources, biodiversity/ecosystems, circular economy) and S2–S3 (workers in the value chain, affected communities); E3 and S3 were included in identification but assessed non-material in subsequent double materiality.
- Risk assessment and measurement (ERM step 3) occur at multiple levels:
  - Bank level: climate and environmental risks are embedded in internal stress testing.
  - Portfolio level: scenario analyses (in 2024 for residential and commercial real estate) and product approval/review processes incorporate sustainability risks.
  - Client level: three tools are used—CASY (for corporate clients with lending > EUR 1 million) to check compliance with the Sustainability Risk Framework; TRA to gauge transition readiness in climate-strategy sectors; and RCT to classify vulnerability to climate and environmental risks. CASY and RCT outputs feed credit assessment, second-line validation, and decisions.
- In 2024, the CASY tool was enhanced to strengthen sector-specific ESG risk assessment against Generic Principles, with tailored requirements for higher-risk sectors; sectors are assigned risk levels across six ESG themes, enabling more granular, better-informed client evaluations where social and environmental/climate risks may differ by sector.
text:
The risk identification part of the ERM cycle relies to a large extent on our Environmental and Social Risk heatmaps. 
These heatmaps inform, for example, the CER materiality assessment, the CER stress testing and the risk appetite . 
Alongside our risk heatmaps, we scan our emerging risks on a quarterly basis. Risks identified as most material 
following the emerging risk scan and assessment with our internal expert stakeholder group feed into our Risk Event 
Register (RER), which subsequently informs our risk taxonomy and scenario booklet.
The Environmental and Social Risk heatmaps identify sub-sectors’ inherent sensitivity to sustainability events. These 
are sub-sectors in which we operate through our corporate lending and residential real estate portfolios (i.e. business 
environment). The business environment is analysed under both a sectoral lens (64 distinct sub-sectors) and a 
geographical lens (regions and countries to which we have exposure, either directly or through sub-sectors’ value 
chains).
The sensitivities in the Overview of environmental and social risk heatmaps for corporate loans are based on the sector 
sensitivities to more than 40 potential underlying physical, transition and negative impact events and focus on our 
corporate lending activities in the downstream part of the value chain. Examples of these events include flooding and 
water stress for physical events, policy and market effects for transition events, and greenhouse gas emissions and
