title: Transmission channel framework
heading: 7.3.30 Transmission channel framework
start_phrase: Transmission channels are the causal chains through which climate factors translate into financial risks to ABN AMRO by directly influencing our counterparties and the assets they hold.
summary:
- Focus on integrating sustainability into client dialogues and credit processes, including offering sustainable home financing and continuously safeguarding proper business conduct.
- Overview of tools used to assess sustainability risks for corporate clients:
  - Transition Readiness Assessment (TRA): first-line engagement tool evaluating clients’ climate performance, transition plans, and ABN AMRO’s ability to support; potential integration into the credit risk process by the second line.
  - Client Assessment on Sustainability (CASY): assessment at onboarding and periodic reviews for lending clients > EUR 1 million, capturing compliance with the bank’s sustainability risk framework and rating outcomes (above/on/below par) to guide further engagement.
  - CER Risk Classification Tool (RCT): classifies non-programme lending clients by physical climate, transition, and environmental risk exposure; integrates CER risk into origination and review creditworthiness assessments and enables data reuse within credit risk.
  - Transmission Channel Framework (TCF): maps how physical and transition risks translate into financial impacts and client creditworthiness; enhanced assessments for high-emitting sectors (agriculture/forestry/fishing, extraction/oil & gas, manufacturing metals & chemicals, power/new energies, construction, shipping/air/road transport, real estate); early-stage incorporation into credit proposals.
- Credit Risk Sustainability (second line of defence) governance and escalation:
  - Oversees due diligence and engagement for lending and non-lending clients; provides KYC sustainability risk advice triggered by adverse media, defence-related activities, and potential breaches of the Exclusion or Controversial Weapons lists.
  - For high-risk lending clients with exposure > EUR 1 million, second-line validation is required; clients may be accepted with conditions if committed to compliance, monitored annually; persistent non-compliance can lead to negative advice and potential relationship exit as a last resort. Non-compliance is treated as a credit risk driver.
- Governance of sustainability matters:
  - Executive Board defines strategy and ensures sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities are addressed across the bank.
  - Supervisory Board oversees and advises on sustainability policies and general affairs.
  - Board committees support governance with defined mandates and procedural rules; reference to broader composition and diversity details in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
text:
Transmission channel framework
Transmission channels are the causal chains through which climate factors translate into financial risks to ABN AMRO 
by directly influencing our counterparties and the assets they hold. Physical risk, such as floods or drought, can lead to 
loss of productivity for companies and to property damage for consumers. In the short term, transition risk is expected 
to lead to higher costs for companies transitioning to a carbon-free environment. The transition may also result in 
some companies’ business models becoming obsolete or to a significant drop in demand. For consumers, transition 
risk may lead to a fall in the prices of properties with low energy labels. The Transmission Channel Framework (TCF) 
aims to capture the possible financial impact arising from these sustainability risks that clients are exposed to, which 
could have an impact on the client’s creditworthiness, and ultimately, the bank’s profit and loss. Reflecting these risks, 
we improved the transmission channel assessments for the following sectors1, which have been assessed 
as contributing highly to climate change:
•Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing (A01-A03)
•Extraction, Oil & Gas (B05-B09)
•Manufacturing Metals & Chemicals (C10-C33)
•New Energies (Power- D35)
•Construction (F41-F43)
•Shipping, Air & Road transport (H49-H51)ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
2101  Sectors refer to ABN AMRO internal definitions, and the indicated NACE codes serve as a proxy only.•Real Estate (L68)
In this developing discipline, the ultimate goal is to have a better understanding of the possible impact of sustainability 
risks on the creditworthiness of the client (outside-in perspective), how to manage/mitigate them and incorporate the 
assessment in the credit proposal and review. We are at the early stages of this process with the help of our above 
mentioned tools.

title: Credit Risk Sustainability team
heading: 7.3.31 Credit Risk Sustainability team
start_phrase: Credit Risk Sustainability, as part of the second line of defence, oversees these client-level due diligence assessments and engagement for both lending and non-lending clients.
summary:
- Developing approach in Real Estate to assess how sustainability risks affect client creditworthiness (outside-in), manage/mitigate those risks, and embed findings into credit proposals and reviews; currently in early stages supported by internal tools.
- Credit Risk Sustainability team acts as second line of defence, overseeing client-level sustainability due diligence and engagement for both lending and non-lending clients.
- Sustainability risk advice can be triggered via KYC by adverse sustainability-related media, defence-related activities, or potential breaches of the bank’s Exclusion List or Controversial Weapons List.
- For lending clients with high sustainability risk and exposure above EUR 1 million, a second-line opinion is required to validate first-line assessments against the bank’s sustainability risk framework.
- Clients not fully compliant but showing credible commitment and capacity may be conditionally accepted with requirements and annual monitoring; non-compliance is treated as a credit risk driver affecting creditworthiness or collateral.
- If a client lacks compliance and sufficient capacity/commitment, the second line issues negative advice and may recommend exiting the relationship; such exits are a last resort under the bank’s inclusive strategy.
- Governance of sustainability matters centers on processes, controls, and oversight by the Executive Board and Supervisory Board.
- Executive Board sets overall strategy, oversees execution of material sustainability matters, and ensures strategy addresses sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Supervisory Board oversees Executive Board policies and general affairs, and advises on sustainability.
- Executive Board committees support with diverse perspectives per their mandates; both the Board and its committees operate under defined procedural rules.
text:
Credit Risk Sustainability team
Credit Risk Sustainability, as part of the second line of defence, oversees these client-level due diligence assessments 
and engagement for both lending and non-lending clients. In the context of KYC processes, sustainability risk advice 
can be provided for lending and non-lending clients, and is triggered by adverse sustainability-related media hits, 
defence-related activities and/or a potential violation of the bank’s Exclusion List or Controversial Weapons List.
For lending clients with a high sustainability risk level and total lending exposure in excess of EUR 1 million, an 
additional second-line advice is required from Credit Risk Sustainability. This provides validation on the first line 
assessments against the bank’s sustainability risk framework. 
If a client is not fully compliant with the sustainability risk framework, but demonstrates sufficient commitment and 
capacity to comply, the second line may accept the client relationship/line of credit, subject to conditions aimed at 
establishing that a client is moving towards full compliance with the sustainability risk framework. Non-compliance is 
then considered a driver of credit risk that could lead to the deterioration of a counterparty’s creditworthiness or 
collateral due to physical and transition risk or prosecution for health and safety breaches. These clients are monitored 
annually. 
If a client is not compliant with the sustainability risk framework and does not demonstrate sufficient capacity or 
commitment to achieve compliance, the sustainability risk advice will be negative and the credit committee may be 
advised to consider exiting the relationship from a sustainability perspective. Given the bank’s inclusive strategy, this 
type of negative conclusion is a last-resort risk response.

This section sets out the governance processes, controls and procedures put in place to monitor, manage and oversee

title: Composition
heading: 7.4.1 Composition
start_phrase: To govern ESG matters effectively, the Executive Board and Supervisory Board must be equipped with the right tools to make the best possible decisions for the short, medium and long-term resilience of ABN AMRO and the wider society in which we operate.
summary:
- Emphasis on integrating sustainability risks into credit risk assessments for Real Estate (L68), aiming to understand how sustainability factors affect client creditworthiness (outside-in), how to manage/mitigate them, and how to embed findings in credit proposals and reviews; process is in early stages with supporting tools.
- Credit Risk Sustainability team functions as the second line of defence, overseeing client-level sustainability due diligence and engagement for both lending and non-lending clients, including within KYC. Triggers include adverse sustainability-related media, defence-related activities, and potential breaches of the Exclusion List or Controversial Weapons List.
- For lending clients with high sustainability risk and exposure above EUR 1 million, second-line advice is required to validate first-line assessments against the bank’s sustainability risk framework.
- Clients not fully compliant but showing capacity and commitment to comply may be accepted with conditions aimed at achieving full compliance; non-compliance is treated as a credit risk driver (e.g., from physical/transition risks or legal breaches) and such clients are monitored annually.
- Clients not compliant and lacking capacity/commitment receive negative sustainability advice, and the credit committee may be advised to exit the relationship; exits are positioned as a last resort in line with the bank’s inclusive strategy.
- Governance of sustainability matters details processes, controls, and oversight, focusing on the Executive Board (EB) and Supervisory Board (SB).
- Composition highlights the need for appropriate tools and expertise for effective ESG oversight; further details on EB/SB composition and diversity are referenced in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Roles and responsibilities: the EB defines overall strategy and oversees integration of material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities across the bank; the SB supervises EB policies and general affairs and advises on sustainability matters.
- EB committees support with diverse perspectives per their mandates; procedural rules guide the functioning of the EB and each committee.
text:
Composition
To govern ESG matters effectively, the Executive Board and Supervisory Board must be equipped with the right tools 
to make the best possible decisions for the short, medium and long-term resilience of ABN AMRO and the wider 
society in which we operate.
For further information on the composition and diversity of the Executive Board and Supervisory Board, please refer to 
the Leadership & governance section of the Integrated Annual Report 2024.

title: Roles and responsibilities
heading: 7.4.2 Roles and responsibilities
start_phrase: The Executive Board is responsible for defining ABN AMRO’s overall strategy.
summary:
- Focus on integrating sustainability risk into credit risk processes, with an outside-in perspective on how sustainability risks affect client creditworthiness, collateral, and credit proposals/reviews; discipline is developing with new tools.
- Credit Risk Sustainability team acts as second line of defence, overseeing client-level sustainability due diligence and engagement for both lending and non-lending clients.
- Sustainability risk advice in KYC is triggered by adverse sustainability-related media, defence-related activities, or potential breaches of the bank’s Exclusion List/Controversial Weapons List.
- For lending clients with high sustainability risk and total exposure > EUR 1 million, second-line advice is required to validate first-line assessments against the bank’s sustainability risk framework.
- Clients not fully compliant but showing capacity and commitment can be conditionally accepted, with non-compliance treated as a credit risk driver (e.g., physical/transition risks, health and safety prosecution) and subject to annual monitoring.
- Clients neither compliant nor committed receive negative sustainability advice, and exit may be recommended as a last-resort action under the bank’s inclusive strategy.
- Governance section outlines how sustainability matters are overseen: the Executive Board defines strategy and ensures sustainability impacts, risks and opportunities are addressed; the Supervisory Board supervises policies, general affairs, and advises on sustainability.
- Executive Board committees provide specialized input on sustainability; both the Board and its committees operate under defined procedural rules; composition and diversity details are referenced in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
text:
Roles and responsibilities
The Executive Board is responsible for defining ABN AMRO’s overall strategy. It oversees the implementation and 
execution of material sustainability matters throughout the bank. The Executive Board is also responsible for ensuring 
that the strategy is informed by and addresses sustainability impacts, risks and opportunities. 
The Supervisory Board, in turn, supervises the policies set by the Executive Board, ABN AMRO’s general affairs and the 
connected business. The Supervisory Board also assists the Executive Board by providing advice on sustainability 
matters. 
To carry out its duties, the Executive Board is assisted by its committees, which offer diverse perspectives on 
sustainability matters, depending on their specific mandates. The Executive Board’s procedural rules guide its 
functioning and internal organisation. Each Executive Board committee also has its own procedural rules.ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
211

title: The Group Sustainability Committee (GSC)
heading: 7.4.3 The Group Sustainability Committee (GSC)
start_phrase: The Group Sustainability Committee (GSC) is an Executive Board committee for central oversight and steering on sustainability.
summary:
- Establishes ABN AMRO’s sustainability governance architecture and committee roles across Executive and Supervisory levels.
- Details the Group Sustainability Committee (GSC) as the central oversight and steering body for sustainability, channeling material information, advising the Executive Board, and embedding double materiality and ESRS considerations.
- Outlines GSC duties: shaping strategy, policies, and standards for long‑term value creation; determining actual/potential impacts on people and environment; guiding sustainability KPIs, metrics, and due diligence; monitoring internal/external stakeholder dialogues; advising on values, conduct, culture, and D&I; and overseeing sustainability commitments.
- Describes the Group Disclosure Committee (GDC) as responsible for the accuracy, effectiveness, and timeliness of sustainability disclosures under Dutch and EU law, serving as the central disclosure hub for material matters.
- Assigns the Group Risk Committee (GRC) responsibility for sustainability risk management within risk appetite, including assessing short-, medium-, and long-term environmental and social risks, reviewing climate/environmental risks and sectoral financing policies with targets and limits, and evaluating interdependencies with reputational, legal, credit, and business risks.
- Notes the Central Credit Committee (CCC) integrates ESG risks into credit decisions, ensuring individual transactions align with policies, standards, and the bank’s risk appetite.
- Explains Supervisory Board oversight: the Supervisory Sustainability Committee supervises strategy and policies (including ESRS topics), while Risk & Capital and Audit Committees coordinate and collaborate—also ad hoc—to ensure comprehensive risk coverage.
- Clarifies the Audit Committee’s role in supervising financial and sustainability reporting integrity and quality, including external disclosures.
- Emphasizes continuous enhancement of sustainability governance to embed sustainability across the organization, align with evolving regulation and market practices.
- Highlights the Sustainability Centre of Excellence, led by the Chief Sustainability Officer reporting to the CEO, which implements new sustainability reporting regulations, sets metrics, and validates targets against ambition levels.
text:
The Group Sustainability Committee (GSC) is an Executive Board committee for central oversight and steering on 
sustainability. It serves as a central point to which material information is directed on topics that relate to sustainability. 
The GSC assists the Executive Board and its committees on matters that relate to sustainability oversight, including in 
relation to material impacts under ESRS as defined by the double materiality assessment. All relevant departments of 
the bank are represented within the GSC. The Executive Board has mandated this committee to assist, advise and 
support in the performance of its duties regarding sustainability-related matters. This includes sustainability aspects of 
the bank’s strategy, policies and standards for various topics to drive and develop a view on sustainable long-term 
value creation, and formulate specific objectives in line with its mandate. Additionally, the GSC determines the actual 
and potential effects that ABN AMRO and its affiliated enterprises have on people and the environment. It monitors 
dialogues about sustainability implementation both with internal and external stakeholders. It also formulates 
guidance on sustainability KPIs, metrics and due diligence obligations regarding ABN AMRO’s operations. The GSC 
advises on ABN AMRO’s values, conduct, culture, and diversity and inclusion matters. It has also established a process 
for entering into and overseeing sustainability commitments.

title: The Group Disclosure Committee (GDC)
heading: 7.4.4 The Group Disclosure Committee (GDC)
start_phrase: The responsibilities of the Group Disclosure Committee (GDC) include advising and supporting the Executive Board in maintaining the accuracy, effectiveness and timeliness of disclosures relating to sustainability matters, including performance on social and environmental impacts, as mandated by Dutch and European law.
summary:
- Describes ABN AMRO’s sustainability governance framework centered on Executive Board and Supervisory Board oversight.
- Explains the Group Sustainability Committee (GSC) as the executive-level body for central sustainability oversight: channels material sustainability information; supports strategy, policies, and standards; applies ESRS double materiality; determines actual and potential impacts on people and the environment; guides KPIs, metrics, and due diligence; oversees stakeholder dialogues; advises on values, conduct, culture, and D&I; and manages sustainability commitments. All relevant bank departments are represented.
- Outlines the Group Disclosure Committee (GDC) role in ensuring accurate, effective, and timely sustainability disclosures in line with Dutch and EU law, acting as the central disclosure point on material matters.
- Details the Group Risk Committee (GRC) mandate for sustainability risk management: reviewing the risk profile within risk appetite; assessing short-, medium-, and long-term environmental and social risks; reviewing climate/environmental risks and sectoral financing policies (targets and limits); quantifying and monitoring environmental risks over the long term; and evaluating interdependencies among sustainability, reputational, legal, credit, and business risks, including those tied to climate strategy.
- Notes the Central Credit Committee (CCC) integrates ESG risks into credit decisions, approving or rejecting transactions to ensure alignment with policies, standards, and risk appetite.
- Covers Supervisory Board oversight: the Supervisory Sustainability Committee supervises sustainability aspects of strategy and policies (including ESRS topics), coordinating with the Risk & Capital Committee and the Audit Committee to capture and assess relevant risks; ad hoc collaboration is used when needed.
- States the Audit Committee monitors the integrity and quality of sustainability reporting and external disclosures alongside financial reporting.
- Emphasizes continuous enhancement of sustainability governance to meet regulatory expectations and evolving market practices.
- Highlights the Sustainability Centre of Excellence, led by the Chief Sustainability Officer reporting to the CEO, which implements new sustainability reporting regulations, owns related processes, determines metrics, and validates targets against ambition levels.
text:
The responsibilities of the Group Disclosure Committee (GDC) include advising and supporting the Executive Board in 
maintaining the accuracy, effectiveness and timeliness of disclosures relating to sustainability matters, including 
performance on social and environmental impacts, as mandated by Dutch and European law. In essence, the GDC 
serves as the central point for disclosing information on material matters regarding the bank and its operating 
environment.

title: The Group Risk Committee (GRC)
heading: 7.4.5 The Group Risk Committee (GRC)
start_phrase: The Group Risk Committee (GRC) is responsible for sustainability risk management, for carrying the mandate to review and for steering ABN AMRO’s risk profile within the scope of the bank’s risk appetite.
summary:
- Describes ABN AMRO’s sustainability governance framework, detailing roles and interactions among Executive Board, Supervisory Board, and key committees.
- Group Sustainability Committee (GSC): Executive Board committee providing central oversight and steering on sustainability; receives material sustainability information; advises on ESRS double materiality matters; represents all bank departments; supports strategy, policies, standards, and long-term value creation; assesses actual and potential impacts on people and environment; oversees stakeholder dialogues; sets guidance for sustainability KPIs, metrics, and due diligence; advises on values, conduct, culture, and D&I; manages processes for sustainability commitments.
- Group Disclosure Committee (GDC): Ensures accurate, effective, and timely sustainability disclosures under Dutch/EU law; central point for disclosing material matters on social and environmental performance.
- Group Risk Committee (GRC): Manages sustainability risk within risk appetite; evaluates short-, medium-, and long-term environmental and social risks; reviews climate/environmental risks and sectoral financing policies with targets and limits; identifies and quantifies environmental risks over long horizons; assesses interdependencies with reputational, legal, credit, and business risks linked to climate strategy.
- Central Credit Committee (CCC): Integrates ESG risks into credit decisions; approves/rejects credit proposals; ensures transactions align with policies, standards, and risk appetite.
- Supervisory Board oversight: All committees address sustainability within their remit; the Supervisory Sustainability Committee oversees sustainability strategy and policies across ESRS topics; coordinates with the Risk & Capital Committee and Audit Committee, including ad hoc collaboration for comprehensive risk assessment.
- Audit Committee: Supervises financial and sustainability reporting, monitoring the integrity and quality of sustainability statements and external disclosures.
- Continuous enhancement: Ongoing monitoring to embed sustainability in governance, align with evolving regulations and market practices.
- Sustainability Centre of Excellence: Led by the Chief Sustainability Officer reporting to the CEO; implements new sustainability reporting regulations; defines metrics and validates targets against ambition levels.
text:
The Group Risk Committee (GRC) is responsible for sustainability risk management, for carrying the mandate to review 
and for steering ABN AMRO’s risk profile within the scope of the bank’s risk appetite. This committee also evaluates 
the short, medium and long-term effects of environmental and social risks on ABN AMRO to support the Executive 
Board in making informed strategic and business decisions. This includes reviewing climate and environmental risks, 
as well as related sectoral financing policies, which determine both targets and limits for exposures to certain sectors. 
The GRC also identifies and quantifies environmental risks, with a view to managing and monitoring these risks over a 
sufficiently long-term horizon. In addition, it assesses interdependencies between sustainability, reputational, legal, 
credit and business risks, including those related to ABN AMRO’s climate strategy-related initiatives.

The Central Credit Committee (CCC) takes ESG risks into account as part of its credit decisions. The CCC makes 
decisions on the acceptance of credit and counterparty risks relating to credit proposals. As such, it can approve or 
reject requests for individual corporate loans and facilities and determine whether individual transactions are in line 
with our policies and standards. This includes sustainability aspects falling within the scope of the risk appetite 
determined by the Executive Board.

heading: 7.5 Environment
start_phrase: Through our double materiality assessment, we have identified four material environmental topics: climate change, pollution, biodiversity & ecosystems, and resource use & circular economy.
summary:
Environment
 Through our double materiality assessment, we have identified four material environmental topics: climate change, 
pollution, biodiversity & ecosystems, and resource use & circular economy.  The former two have been identified as 
material for risks, and the latter as material from an impact perspective. Below we will focus on the material risks.
text:
Environment
 Through our double materiality assessment, we have identified four material environmental topics: climate change, 
pollution, biodiversity & ecosystems, and resource use & circular economy.  The former two have been identified as 
material for risks, and the latter as material from an impact perspective. Below we will focus on the material risks.

title: Climate-related policies
heading: 7.5.1.1 Climate-related policies
start_phrase: This section outlines the internal policies we have implemented to manage the material impacts, risks and opportunities in our value chain related to climate change.
summary:
- The Environment section identifies four material topics via a double materiality assessment: climate change and pollution (material for risk), and biodiversity & ecosystems and resource use & circular economy (material for impact). The section focuses on material risks.
- Climate risk governance: Integrated into ABN AMRO’s risk taxonomy, risk appetite, and financial planning under sustainability risk, managed through the enterprise risk management cycle via a sustainability risk policy framework.
- Policies and standards: Framework addresses climate change mitigation and management of physical and transition risks, with ongoing development to better manage impacts and opportunities across the value chain.
- Operational management: 
  - Environmental and Energy Policy aims to cut building energy use and increase renewable energy through procurement; overseen by the COO.
  - Travel and Mobility Policy focuses on electrifying the lease fleet, reducing business travel emissions, and promoting alternative travel; overseen by the CHRO.
  - Current scope is the Netherlands, with plans to extend to other countries.
- Climate strategy (launched Dec 2022): Aligns with limiting warming to 1.5°C and net zero by 2050; guided by the Dutch Financial Sector Climate Agreement and the Net-Zero Banking Alliance (NZBA), prioritizing sector-specific targets for high-emitting industries.
- Sector coverage: No specific targets for iron & steel, aluminium, cement, and aviation due to limited exposure, but continued monitoring and client support for decarbonisation.
- Three decarbonisation levers:
  1) Client engagement and financing solutions, including a Transition Readiness Assessment tool covering most of the climate strategy portfolio across six sectors and ~2,100 clients in 2024.
  2) Alignment of processes and policies with net-zero targets, embedded in credit approval and capital allocation; updated standards for coal-fired power generation include client requirements to phase out thermal coal by 2030.
  3) Engagement with industry and governments to promote sector-wide transitions and support clients’ pathways to net zero.
text:
Climate-related policies
This section outlines the internal policies we have implemented to manage the material impacts, risks and 
opportunities in our value chain related to climate change.
At ABN AMRO, climate risk is integrated into our risk taxonomy, risk appetite and financial planning under 
sustainability risk. Our sustainability risk policy framework ensures that environmental risks are managed throughout 
the enterprise risk management cycle.
Our climate strategy supplements this framework by setting targets and initiatives to align our portfolio and operations 
with a net-zero trajectory and reduce GHG emissions. Various policies and standards manage climate risks.  Our 
sustainability risk policy framework addresses climate change mitigation and the management of physical and 
transition risk, while also helping us to address our broader climate impacts. We are continuing to assess how to 
further develop our policies relating to the management of impacts and opportunities in the future.

title: Managing our operations
heading: 7.5.1.2 Managing our operations
start_phrase: We aim to reduce the climate impact of our own operations.

- Decarbonisation levers:
  1) Client engagement and finance solutions, including a Transition Readiness Assessment across six sectors, covering about 2,100 clients in 2024.
  2) Alignment of internal processes and policies with net-zero goals, reflected in credit approval and capital allocation; updated sustainability risk standards for coal-fired power, committing to phase out thermal coal by 2030.

text:
Managing our operations
We aim to reduce the climate impact of our own operations. To achieve this, we have adopted policies targeting 
carbon emissions and energy use. The Environmental and Energy Policy is designed to reduce energy usage in our 
buildings and increase the use of renewable energy through changes to procurement practices. The Chief Operations 
Officer (COO) oversees the implementation of the policy. Similarly, the Travel and Mobility policy is focused on 
electrifying our lease fleet, reducing emissions from business travel, and encouraging alternative travel options. 
Implementation of this policy is overseen by the CHRO.
While these policies currently apply to operations in the Netherlands, we are working on extending them to other 
countries .

title: Climate strategy
heading: 7.5.1.3 Climate strategy
start_phrase: Our climate strategy, introduced in December 2022, defines our approach to aligning with the global goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C and supporting the transition to a net-zero economy by 2050.
summary:
- The document section covers ABN AMRO’s environmental focus areas identified via a double materiality assessment: climate change, pollution (material as risks), and biodiversity & ecosystems plus resource use & circular economy (material from an impact perspective), with this excerpt focusing on climate-related risks.

  1) Client engagement and financing solutions, including a Transition Readiness Assessment tool covering most of the climate strategy portfolio across six sectors and about 2,100 clients in 2024.
  2) Aligning internal processes and policies with net-zero targets, integrating climate into credit approval and capital allocation; updated sustainability risk standards now require phasing out thermal coal by 2030 for coal-fired power generation clients.

text:
Climate strategy
Our climate strategy, introduced in December 2022, defines our approach to aligning with the global goal of limiting 
global warming to 1.5°C and supporting the transition to a net-zero economy by 2050. As part of our commitments 
under the Dutch Financial Sector Climate Agreement and the NZBA, we have prioritised sector-specific targets for 
high-emitting industries. The NZBA framework provides internationally recognised, science-based guidance for our 
decarbonisation efforts. 
For sectors such as iron & steel, aluminium, cement and aviation, we have determined that our current financial 
exposure is not significant enough to set specific targets. However, we will continue to monitor these sectors and work 
with corporate clients to support their decarbonisation efforts.
This year, building on the priorities from our 2022 climate strategy, we have identified three decarbonisation levers 
that ABN AMRO uses to implement specific actions aimed at achieving climate targets for each sector. First, we 
engage with clients and offer financing solutions to support their journey to net zero . One example is our Transition 
Readiness Assessment tool , covering the majority of our climate strategy portfolio across six sectors and involving 
approximately 2,100 clients in 2024. Second, we ensure our processes and policies are aligned with net zero targets, 
enabling us to assess risks and challenges to meeting reduction targets and transition risks. This alignment is reflected 
in credit approval and capital allocation processes, which are continually evolving. A notable update in this respect is 
that we have updated the requirements for coal-fired power generation companies in the sustainability risk standard 
with client requirements, which commits to phasing out thermal coal by 2030. Lastly, we engage with industry and 
governments to raise awareness and promote sector-wide change, thus reinforcing our dedication to supporting our 
clients in their transitions.ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡

title: How the targets were set
heading: 7.5.1.4.1 How the targets were set
start_phrase: We have set emission reduction targets and ambitions across our lending portfolios, operational activities and client asset portfolios, with a focus on responsibly reducing carbon intensity.
summary:
- Describes ABN AMRO’s methodology for setting emission-reduction targets across lending portfolios, operations, and client asset portfolios, focused on lowering carbon intensity.
- Targets were set without external stakeholder involvement and rest on three pillars: alignment with NZBA and PCAF guidelines, a science-based approach using recognized scenarios, and a sector-based focus prioritizing carbon‑intensive industries.
- Assumptions include the maturation of emerging technologies and shifts in consumer demand; targets have not been externally validated.
- For assets under management, the ISS framework is used, with an objective to reduce the Weighted Average Carbon Intensity (WACI) of clients’ portfolios, specifically equities in DPM mandates.
- Client engagement is central to the transition strategy, embedded in risk assessment, measurement, and response processes.
- Materiality is defined by exposure: sectors with drawn exposure below 0.25% of the corporate loan book are deemed immaterial.
- Baselines are calculated using single-year data (not older than two years), with any significant subsequent changes to be reported.
- Published targets cover key NZBA carbon-intensive sectors—agriculture, commercial and residential real estate, oil and gas, power generation, and transport—representing 95% of exposure to NZBA sectors; the remaining 5% will be addressed in future updates or excluded due to methodological constraints.
- No specific targets for iron & steel, aluminium, and cement due to minimal exposure (<1% combined; <0.25% each), though exposures will be monitored and clients engaged.
- Sector decarbonisation pathways differ by portfolio characteristics; most sectors use 1.5°C-aligned benchmarks (CRREM, IEA, DNV), covering 93% of NZBA-sector exposure, while agriculture follows the Netherlands’ KEV 2022 (PBL) approach using IPCC AR5 GWP and reflecting Dutch/EU policy.
text:
How the targets were set
We have set emission reduction targets and ambitions across our lending portfolios, operational activities and client 
asset portfolios, with a focus on responsibly reducing carbon intensity.  No external stakeholders were involved in the 
target-setting process. Our approach to target-setting for the lending portfolio is built on three key elements:
•Industry guidelines: We align our targets with industry best practices, following guidelines such as the NZBA 
Climate Target Setting for Banks and the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF) methodological 
guidance. This ensures our targets are consistent with our commitments to the NZBA and PCAF.
•Science-based approach: Targets are grounded in the methodologies, decarbonisation scenarios and data currently 
available, adhering to NZBA guidance. 
•Sector-based focus: We adopt a sector-based approach to target-setting, recognising that each sector in the 
economy faces unique challenges in transitioning to net zero. By prioritising carbon-intensive sectors, as 
recommended by the NZBA, we aim to drive the most impactful decarbonisation of our portfolio. 
To achieve our targets we rely on assumptions embedded in the underlying benchmarks, including the development 
of emerging technologies and shifts in consumer demand. The climate targets have not been validated by an 
independent external body. For setting ambitions related to our assets under management, we use the Institutional 
Shareholder Services (ISS) framework to guide our approach in measuring the climate impact within our investment 
portfolios. Our objective is to reduce the Weighted Average Carbon Intensity (WACI) of our clients’ investment 
portfolios, specifically within the equity holdings of our DPM mandates.

title: Client engagement
heading: 7.5.1.5 Client engagement
start_phrase: Engaging with clients to support their transition to net zero is a cornerstone of our climate strategy and a critical component of our decarbonisation efforts.
summary:
- The document outlines ABN AMRO’s climate target-setting approach across lending portfolios, operational activities, and client asset portfolios, focusing on reducing carbon intensity.
- Targets are designed without external stakeholder involvement and have not been independently validated.
- Target-setting is based on three pillars: alignment with industry guidelines (NZBA Climate Target Setting for Banks and PCAF), adherence to science-based methodologies and scenarios per NZBA guidance, and a sector-based focus prioritizing carbon‑intensive sectors.
- Assumptions within sector benchmarks include expected advances in emerging technologies and shifts in consumer demand.
- For assets under management, ABN AMRO uses the ISS framework and aims to lower the Weighted Average Carbon Intensity (WACI) of clients’ investment portfolios, specifically the equity holdings in Discretionary Portfolio Management mandates.
- Client engagement is central to the bank’s decarbonisation strategy, integrated with risk assessment and response processes.
- Materiality is defined by sector exposure; sectors with drawn exposures below 0.25% of the corporate loan book are treated as immaterial.
- Baseline values for targets use single‑year data (not older than two years) per NZBA recommendations; significant subsequent changes will be disclosed.
- Targets are set for key NZBA carbon‑intensive sectors: agriculture, commercial and residential real estate, oil and gas, power generation, and transport.
- Current targets cover 95% of exposure to NZBA carbon‑intensive sectors; the remaining 5% will be addressed in future updates or is excluded due to methodological constraints.
- No specific targets are set for iron & steel, aluminium, and cement due to limited exposure (each <0.25%, combined <1%); the bank will continue monitoring and engaging with clients in these sectors.
- Decarbonisation pathways differ by sector based on portfolio and emissions characteristics; for all sectors except agriculture and client assets, targets align with 1.5°C pathways (e.g., CRREM, IEA, DNV), covering 93% of NZBA sector exposure.

text:
Client engagement
Engaging with clients to support their transition to net zero is a cornerstone of our climate strategy and a critical 
component of our decarbonisation efforts.  Risk assessment and measurement and Risk response sections above 
explain how we engage with our clients.

title: Overview of sectors and targets
heading: 7.5.1.6 Overview of sectors and targets
start_phrase: ABN AMRO has set targets for carbon-intensive sectors that are material and significant to our organisation.
summary:
- Scope and aim of targets: Emission reduction targets set across lending portfolios, operational activities, and client asset portfolios to responsibly cut carbon intensity; no external stakeholders involved.
- Target-setting pillars: 
  - Alignment with industry guidelines (NZBA Climate Target Setting for Banks, PCAF methodology).
  - Science-based methods and decarbonisation scenarios per NZBA guidance.
  - Sector-based focus prioritising carbon‑intensive sectors for maximum impact.
  - Reliance on benchmark assumptions; targets not externally validated.
- Client assets approach: Use of ISS framework to measure climate impact; objective to lower WACI in equity holdings within DPM mandates.
- Client engagement: Central to transition strategy; engagement embedded in risk assessment, measurement, and response processes.
- Sector coverage and materiality:
  - Materiality defined by exposure; sectors with <0.25% of corporate loan book deemed immaterial.
  - Baselines use single-year data (no older than two years), with future significant changes to be reported.
  - Targets set for NZBA carbon‑intensive sectors (agriculture, commercial and residential real estate, oil & gas, power generation, transport), covering 95% of exposure; remaining 5% to be added later or excluded due to methods.
  - No specific targets for iron & steel, aluminium, cement due to immaterial exposure (<1% combined); ongoing monitoring and engagement continue.
- Pathways and benchmarks:
  - Sector-specific decarbonisation pathways vary by portfolio and product.
  - 1.5°C‑aligned benchmarks (CRREM, IEA, DNV) used for all except agriculture and client assets, covering 93% of exposure.
  - Agriculture aligned with Dutch KEV 2022 (PBL) using IPCC AR5 GWPs and Fit for 55 policy context; agriculture is 2% of NZBA exposure.
  - Client assets scenario not yet science‑based.
  - Full 1.5°C alignment not required by 2030 for residential mortgages, inland shipping, and road transport (trucks/vans); interim targets may sit above benchmark.
- 2024 developments: Second year of climate strategy; continued portfolio management and commercial initiatives; entry into refinement phase with target updates based on new data, insights, and methodologies; progress reported in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Climate risk management:
  - Climate change treated as a material risk within risk taxonomy and appetite under sustainability risk.
  - Periodic measurement/monitoring to assess alignment of client portfolios with strategy.
- Climate risk heatmap:
  - Assesses sector sensitivity to physical and transition risks and potential negative impacts.
  - Physical risk inputs: CAS Climate Impact Atlas and Encore for Dutch flooding (2050 projections); Moody’s ESG Solutions for other hazards/geographies (2040), using high-emissions RCP 8.5.
  - Transition risk drivers: sector GHG intensity (PCAF, ISS Oekom) plus regulatory, technological, and market parameters; regulatory references include Dutch Climate Agreement (to 2030) and Environmental Performance Index country targets.
  - Highest sensitivities found in agriculture (NACE A), mining (B), manufacturing (C), power generation (D), and transport (H); detailed heatmap in the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Risk mitigation and scenarios: Climate risk mitigated via established risk response processes; scenario analysis focuses on Dutch‑concentrated loan book with physical risk assessment across corporate loans and residential mortgages using regional (NUTS) granularity.
text:
Overview of sectors and targets
ABN AMRO has set targets for carbon-intensive sectors that are material and significant to our organisation. Our 
approach is to define materiality by assessing sector exposures, considering sectors with drawn exposures of less than 
0.25% of the corporate loan book as immaterial. For transparency reasons, all sector baseline values calculated are 
based on data from a single year, rather than on multi-year averages. This approach aligns with NZBA 
recommendations, which specify that baseline data should be no older than two years. Any subsequent significant 
changes to the baseline, such as those resulting from external factors or portfolio adjustments, will be reported.
In line with our climate strategy and our commitment to NZBA, we have set and published targets for several of the 
NZBA carbon-intensive sectors (agriculture, commercial and residential real estate, oil and gas, power generation, and 
transport). Our targets currently cover 95%  of our total exposure to NZBA carbon-intensive sectors, based on the 
outstanding exposure captured (in gross carrying amount) by our climate targets divided by the exposure to the NZBA 
carbon-intensive sectors. The remaining 5%, which is not yet covered by a target, will either be incorporated into 
subsequent updates of our climate strategy or is excluded due to methodological assumptions . 
We have chosen not to set specific targets for certain NZBA sectors because of their limited materiality. These sectors 
— iron & steel, aluminium and cement — make up a very small part of our exposure, collectively representing less 
than 1% of our total exposure to NZBA sectors, with each sector individually contributing less than 0.25%. We remain 
committed to monitoring the exposure to these sectors and will engage with clients in these sectors to support their 
decarbonisation efforts.
With regard to these targets, the selected decarbonisation pathways vary across sectors due to differences in portfolio 
characteristics, emission-generating activities, lending products and the chosen target type. For all sectors apart from 
agriculture and our ambition for client assets, we have chosen science-based benchmarks that are aligned with 1.5°C 
scenario reference pathways (including CRREM, the IEA and DNV), covering 93% of our total exposure to NZBA 
sectors. For agriculture, we have opted to align with the scientific calculations in the 2022 Climate and Energy Outlook 
of the Netherlands (Klimaat- en Energieverkenning, KEV) compiled by the Netherlands Environmental Assessment 
Agency (Planbureau voor de leefomgeving, PBL), which uses the IPCC Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) for GWP values 
and considers the implemented and proposed policies of the Dutch Coalition Agreement and its ability to fulfil the EU ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
215FIT for 55 goals. The agricultural sector accounts for 2% of our total exposure to NZBA sectors. The scenario used for 
client assets is not yet science-based.
 
While we aim for alignment with these pathways, it is important to note that full 1.5°C alignment does not necessarily 
need to be achieved by 2030. This applies to residential mortgages, inland shipping, and road transport trucks and 
vans, where the intermediary target is above the benchmark line.
The year  2024 was the second year since the introduction of our climate strategy, and we continued to manage our 
portfolio and implement commercial initiatives in line with this strategy throughout the year. However, 2024 also 
represented a turning point as we moved into a new phase of our strategy. We are now refining and revising targets to 
reflect new information, such as additional available data, new climate strategy insights and updated methodologies.
For more information on how we are progressing on the targets we have set per sector, please see our Integrated 
Annual Report 2024.

title: Climate risk heatmap
heading: 7.5.1.7.1 Climate risk heatmap

text:
Climate risk heatmap
The environmental and social heatmap relating to climate risk evaluates the sensitivity of various sectors to climate-
related physical and transition risks, including negative impacts. 
For physical risks, sensitivity is based on a combination of sector characteristics, such as dependence on assets, labour 
and ecosystem services, as well as the regional and country-based exposure to hazards (such as flooding, heat stress 
and sea level rise). For our portfolio located in the Netherlands, we source exposure to flooding from the Climate 
Impact Atlas of Climate Adaptation Services (CAS), relying on 2050 projections, as well as from Encore (Exploring 
natural capital opportunities risks and exposure). For other hazards and geographies, we source sensitivity estimations 
from Moody’s ESG Solutions, relying on projections to 2040. Both data sources assume a high emission scenario 
(Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5 scenario). 
Transition risk sensitivity is determined by the sector’s greenhouse gas emission intensity (derived from PCAF and ISS 
Oekom sources), alongside various regulatory, technological and market parameters. The regulatory parameters are 
done at two levels:
•at a sector level, where we reference the annual sector reduction requirements in the Dutch Climate Agreement 
(focusing on projections to 2030)
•at a country level, where we refer to the most recent policy-induced emission reductions targets in the 
Environmental Performance Index
The chart below highlights sectors with moderately high or high sensitivity to one or more of the three key factors: 
physical risk sensitivity, transition risk sensitivity and negative impact. 
The results of the heatmap show that the highest sensitivities (Moderately high and High) are in the agricultural (NACE 
A), mining (NACE B), manufacturing (NACE C), power generation (NACE D) and transport sectors (NACE H).  The climate 
risk h eatmap is available on our Integrated Annual Report 2024.

title: Climate scenario analysis, scenario choice and data
heading: 7.5.1.7.3 Climate scenario analysis, scenario choice and data
start_phrase: Our loans are concentrated in the Netherlands.
summary:
- Strategic context and targets: The bank aims to align with Fit for 55 and NZBA pathways. Agricultural exposures represent 2% of total NZBA sector exposure. The scenario used for client assets is not yet science-based. Full 1.5°C alignment is not expected by 2030 for residential mortgages, inland shipping, and road transport trucks/vans; interim targets in these areas are above benchmark trajectories. 2024 marked the second year of the climate strategy and a transition to a refinement phase, updating targets with new data, insights, and methodologies.

- Climate risk governance and monitoring: Climate change is treated as a material sustainability risk embedded in the risk taxonomy and appetite. The bank periodically measures and monitors climate risk exposure and assesses portfolio alignment with its strategy.

- Climate risk heatmap: Sectoral sensitivity to physical and transition risks and negative impacts is assessed. Physical risk inputs use CAS (Netherlands, 2050) and Encore, plus Moody’s ESG Solutions for other geographies (2040); both assume a high-emissions RCP 8.5 scenario. Transition risk uses GHG intensity (PCAF, ISS Oekom) and regulatory parameters from the Dutch Climate Agreement (to 2030) and the Environmental Performance Index. Sectors with highest sensitivities: agriculture (NACE A), mining (B), manufacturing (C), power generation (D), and transport (H).

- Scenario analysis and data coverage: With lending concentrated in the Netherlands, material physical risk lies in Dutch regions (NUTS). Physical risk assessment covers corporate loans, residential mortgages, and commercial real estate, representing 96% of collateralised loans. In 2024, long-term (to 2050) scenario analyses for residential and commercial real estate assessed physical risks (floods, foundation issues, wildfires, heat stress) and transition risks, incorporating adaptation plans. Flood assumptions follow RCP 8.5 (approx. 4.3°C by 2100). Vulnerable customers are those with high LTV/LTI and/or Stage 2 risk; vulnerable collateral has energy label D or worse and value ≤ EUR 300,000. Impacts on creditworthiness feed into RWA and provision calculations and CER materiality for Credit and Liquidity risks.

- Data sources and methodologies: Foundation risk data from KCAF; other physical hazards from CAS with granular Dutch data. CAS uses KNMI’14 WH scenarios to 2050 and KNMI’23 for flood risk, aligned with NGFS current policies scenario. Results are presented as risk distributions for CRE and RRE across foundation, flood, wildfire, and heat stress, with probabilities bucketed from no risk to high risk (plus no data).

- Risk mitigation: Climate risk is addressed through established risk response processes within overall sustainability risk management.

- Climate-related opportunities and financing: The bank targets up to EUR 1 billion in early-stage capital by 2030 to scale decarbonisation technologies. Cumulative deployed is EUR 333 million since 2022, including EUR 31 million in direct equity and EUR 49 million in fund allocations in 2024. Investments are channeled via direct equity (Sustainable Impact Fund focused on energy transition, built environment, sustainable consumption), climate-focused third-party funds (SFDR Article 8/9), and hybrid debt. Progress is monitored quarterly and mapped to financial statement items (Other equity associates within Equity accounted investments and Financial investments).
text:
Our  loans are concentrated in the Netherlands. Correspondingly, our material physical risk sits mainly in Dutch 
regions (referred to as NUTS, Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics, the geographical division of the economic 
territory in the European Union). Our physical risk assessment covers our corporate loans, residential mortgages and ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
216commercial real estate portfolios and constitutes 96% of our loan book collateralised by physical assets. For 
methodology of our physical risk assessment, please refer to ESG5.
In 2024, we performed climate scenario analyses on our residential and commercial real estate portfolios against 
several long-term (to 2050) climate change scenarios. These analyses assessed physical (e.g. floods, foundation 
problems, wildfires, heat stress) and transition (e.g. policy changes and technological shifts impacting industries) risk 
events and considered risks in climate adaptation plans. The underlying assumptions of the flood assessment reflected 
a high emission scenario (Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5 scenario), where no additional efforts are 
made to constrain greenhouse gas emissions, resulting in a temperature increase of 4.3°C by 2100. The scenario 
analysis for residential real estate also included environmental risk. For the physical risk assessment, customers with 
high loan-to-value and loan-to-income ratios and/or a risk stage 2 (increased risk) classification during the past 
12 months were defined as vulnerable, while collateral with an energy label of D or lower and market value of 
EUR 300,000 or lower was defined as vulnerable. The impact of CER risk events on customers’ creditworthiness was 
assessed and calculated in terms of RWA and provision requirements. The outcomes of the assessment served as an 
input for the Credit and Liquidity risk CER materiality assessments.
Foundation problems are an important driver of physical climate risk in the Dutch real estate sector. Property-specific 
data on foundation risk is available from Kennis Centrum Aanpak Funderingsproblematiek (KCAF), a leading party in 
the Netherlands that generates granular data on this risk. This data is also included in property valuation reports for 
residential real estate. Data on the other drivers of physical climate risk (flooding, wildfires and heat stress) are 
obtained from Climate Adaptation Services (CAS), which provides data for the Netherlands at a highly granular level. 
The CAS data is partly based on the WH scenario to 2050 from the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute (the 
KNMI'14 scenarios). In the case of flood risk, CAS data is based on the new KNMI'23 scenarios. These represent the 
worst-case outcomes for climate change in the Netherlands and closely align with the Network for Greening the 
Financial System (NGFS) current policies scenario.
The climate scenario analysis results as published in our Integrated Annual Report 2024 show the risk distribution of 
our commercial real estate (CRE) and residential real estate (RRE) and portfolio exposures for four climate-related 
risks: foundation risk, flood risk, wildfire risk and heat stress risk. The analysis was performed by measuring the 
chances of the risk events occurring in the years to 2050 for buildings in the Netherlands. The probabilities of 
foundation problems are grouped into five buckets: no risk, low risk, medium risk, high risk and no available data.

title: Investments in equity and hybrid debt
heading: 7.5.1.8.1 Investments in equity and hybrid debt
start_phrase: As part of our climate strategy in 2022, a growth target was established for early-stage capital by 2030.
summary:
- Focus on climate risks in ABN AMRO’s residential and commercial real estate portfolios, which comprise 96% of the loan book collateralised by physical assets; methodology references provided elsewhere (ESG5).
- 2050 climate scenario analyses performed for physical risks (floods, foundation issues, wildfires, heat stress) and transition risks, with residential analysis also covering environmental risk.
- Assumptions include a high-emission RCP 8.5 pathway (≈4.3°C by 2100); flood risk based on KNMI’23 scenarios; other physical risks informed by KNMI’14 WH; alignment with NGFS current policies scenario.
- Data sources: KCAF for foundation risk at property level; CAS for granular Dutch data on flooding, wildfires, and heat stress.
- Vulnerability definitions: clients with high LTV/LTI and/or risk stage 2 in past 12 months; collateral with energy label D or lower and market value ≤ EUR 300,000.
- Credit impact quantified via changes in RWA and provisions; results inform Credit and Liquidity risk climate-environmental risk materiality assessments; risk distributions published for CRE and RRE across four risk types, with foundation risk bucketed from no to high risk plus no-data.
- Climate-related opportunities through equity and hybrid debt: target up to EUR 1 billion in early-stage capital by 2030 to scale decarbonisation technologies; EUR 333 million deployed cumulatively by 2024 (EUR 31 million direct equity; EUR 49 million fund allocations in 2024); investments via Sustainable Impact Fund (energy transition, built environment, sustainable consumption), SFDR Article 8/9 climate funds, and selective hybrid debt.
- Lending to renewables and decarbonisation technologies: initial target ≥ EUR 4 billion by 2025 surpassed with EUR 5.4 billion by end-2024; 2030 target raised to EUR 10 billion; scope includes renewables, hydrogen, storage, clean transport, and related infrastructure; focus on financing companies enabling the energy transition.
- Own operations: ISO 14001-certified EMS with structured governance; net-zero operational emissions by 2030 goal.
- Operational measures: upgrade Dutch offices to energy label A and <50 kWh/m² by 2030; switch to 100% renewable electricity globally; electrify lease car fleets, participate in Anders Reizen Coalition; EV-only lease policies in NL/BE/DE with FR/GR pending, acknowledging potential 2030 emissions from 2025 ICE contracts and pursuing solutions to achieve a fully electric fleet by 2030.
text:
Investments in equity and hybrid debt
As part of our climate strategy in 2022, a growth target was established for early-stage capital by 2030. The energy 
transition requires investing in early-stage companies that have climate change mitigation as a business objective. 
Many technologies that can drive the transition to a low-carbon economy either already exist or are being developed, 
but often face a financing gap between research and development, early-stage adoption and full-scale 
commercialisation. The equity division of corporate banking aims to provide the necessary capital to help these 
technologies scale up to achieve (broader) commercial application. By investing in these scale-up companies, we can 
accelerate the development, deployment and adoption of innovative decarbonisation solutions.
By 2030, up to EUR 1 billion will be allocated to accelerate the transition to a decarbonised economy. We started in 
2022, with EUR 145 million, and the cumulative capital deployed so far totals EUR 333 million. In 2024, we deployed 
EUR 31 million in direct equity and allocated EUR 49 million to fund investments in progressing towards our EUR 1 
billion early-stage capital target. No interim targets for capital deployment by 2030 have yet been set. Progress is 
monitored quarterly by the corporate investments management team, as well as by the climate strategy team. To 
provide clarity on our sustainability metrics, we relate them to key financial statement line items. In the statement of 
financial position these are primarily reflected in Other equity associates within Equity accounted investments and 
Financial investments. This funding is deployed through direct equity, fund investments and hybrid debt. Direct equity 
participations are made via the Sustainable Impact Fund (SIF), which focuses on three areas: the energy transition, built 
environment and sustainable consumption. While SIF emphasises these areas, we also invest in third-party climate-
focused funds to ensure diversification in the climate transition. These are funds that are covered either by Article 8 or 
9 in the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) and whose objective is to address climate change and a just 
transition. Additionally, hybrid debt is offered to a select number of scale-up companies seeking to mitigate climate ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
217change, with the target being innovative firms with near-term positive cash flows, and this assessment is made on a 
case-by-case basis.

title: Renewable energy and decarbonisation technologies
heading: 7.5.1.8.2 Renewable energy and decarbonisation technologies
start_phrase: In 2022, as part of the climate strategy, a target was set for a lending commitment (drawn and undrawn amounts) of at least EUR 4 billion for renewables and decarbonisation technologies by December 2025 to support our clients’ transition to green energy.
summary:
- Focus on financing innovative firms with near-term positive cash flows, assessed case by case.
- Climate strategy includes a lending commitment for renewable energy and decarbonisation technologies: baseline EUR 3.1bn (2022), initial target at least EUR 4bn by December 2025.
- Target exceeded early, reaching EUR 5.4bn in total commitments by end-2024; new 2030 target set at EUR 10bn.
- Progress is monitored quarterly by management and the Group Sustainability Committee.
- Clear methodology defines financing in scope across two components: renewable energy (generation, storage, infrastructure, related services) and decarbonisation technologies (clean fuels, hydrogen, storage, clean transport, and related infrastructure not already counted under renewables).
- Strategic focus on financing companies enabling the energy transition, including renewable generation, low‑carbon hydrogen, clean fuels, energy storage, clean transportation, and supporting infrastructure, leveraging advisory and financing capabilities.
- Operational climate impact primarily from energy use and emissions; the bank remains committed to minimizing its own footprint alongside financed emissions.
- ISO 14001-certified Environmental Management System with assigned ownership of risks/opportunities, stakeholder engagement, monthly climate reviews, and quarterly risk/opportunity assessments.
- Net-zero operational emissions target by 2030, with ongoing measurement, monitoring, and reduction of GHG emissions.
- Buildings: upgrade Dutch offices to energy label A; align with Paris Agreement; target <50 kWh/m²/year by 2030; transition to 100% renewable electricity across all offices while reducing consumption.
- Mobility: electrify lease car fleet; member of Anders Reizen Coalition to reduce commuting and business travel emissions.
- EV-only lease policies implemented in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany; pending in France and Greece; recognition that any new ICE leases in 2025 in pending countries could emit through 2030; active work to achieve a fully electric international lease fleet by 2030.
text:
Renewable energy and decarbonisation technologies
In 2022, as part of the climate strategy, a target was set for a lending commitment (drawn and undrawn amounts) of 
at least EUR 4 billion for renewables and decarbonisation technologies by December 2025 to support our clients’ 
transition to green energy. In 2022, the baseline value of EUR 3.1 billion became part of our climate strategy, and we 
achieved our goal two years ahead of schedule, reaching a total commitment of EUR 5.4 billion by the end of 2024. 
Progress is monitored quarterly by management, as well as in the Group Sustainability Committee. In 2024, we 
increased our target for 2030 to EUR 10 billion.
The methodology to determine the financing in scope encompasses two components: renewable energy and 
decarbonisation technologies. Renewable energy covers activities, assets, infrastructure and projects in the field of and 
companies dedicated to the development, construction, installation, manufacturing, maintenance, operation of and/or 
advice on renewable energy sources and storage techniques. Decarbonisation technologies are activities related to 
renewable energy generation, manufacturing of hydrogen, energy storage, clean transport and infrastructure deals 
across ABN AMRO Corporate Bank’s financing activities and which are not already part of the renewable energy 
component.
To achieve our financing target for new energy, ABN AMRO is focusing on financing companies delivering products 
and services that are key for the energy transition. Leveraging our advisory expertise and financing capabilities, we are 
collaborating with new and existing clients to support a diverse range of solutions, including renewable energy 
generation, manufacturing of clean fuels, low-carbon hydrogen production, energy storage, clean transportation and 
related infrastructure.

title: Our own operations
heading: 7.5.1.9 Our own operations
start_phrase: The primary climate impact of our own operations stems from energy use and carbon emissions generated by day-to-day activities.
summary:
- Focus of financing: target innovative firms with near-term positive cash flows, assessed case by case.
- Renewable energy and decarbonisation financing:
  - 2022 commitment of at least EUR 4 billion (drawn and undrawn) by Dec 2025; baseline EUR 3.1 billion.
  - Achieved EUR 5.4 billion by end-2024, two years early; progress monitored quarterly by management and the Group Sustainability Committee.
  - 2030 target raised to EUR 10 billion.
  - Scope/methodology split into renewable energy (projects, assets, storage) and decarbonisation technologies (hydrogen, energy storage, clean transport, related infrastructure) across Corporate Bank financing.
  - Strategy centers on financing companies delivering key energy-transition products/services, leveraging advisory and financing capabilities.
- Own operations and net-zero by 2030:
  - ISO 14001 Environmental Management System with assigned ownership, monthly climate meetings, and quarterly reviews for risks/opportunities.
  - Buildings: upgrade Dutch offices to energy label A; align with Paris Agreement; <50 kWh/m² by 2030; 100% renewable electricity globally; reduce overall consumption.
  - Mobility/travel: electrify lease fleets (policy active in NL, BE, DE; pending in FR, GR with risk of 2025 non-EV contracts extending emissions to 2030); member of Anders Reizen to cut commuting/business travel emissions; shift short-haul flights to rail; procure sustainable aviation fuel; department-level travel budgets and dashboards; 2023–2024 travel emissions exceeded targets; department-specific reduction plans in progress.
- Nature, pollution, and circular economy:
  - ESRS E2 (air/water pollution), E4 (biodiversity drivers), and E5 (resource use/circular economy) are material from an impact perspective; from a risk perspective, materiality is currently limited to pollution.
- Cross-sector environmental scenario analysis (2023):
  - TNFD-guided, Netherlands-focused transition-risk scenario to 2030; assumes strict implementation/enforcement of EU water/air pollution and nature policies.
  - Used sectoral impact and geographic data to internalize pollution costs and assess permit-related business continuity risks.
  - Key finding: water-pollution costs and continuity risks are highest for manufacturing and agriculture; management overlays applied for Dutch nitrogen measures.
- Forthcoming actions:
  - Integrate environmental risks into stress-testing methodologies and models.
  - Develop an Agriculture Transition Plan for the dairy sub-sector with a 2040 vision, bank ambition/role, and client support actions.
text:
Our own operations
The primary climate impact of our own operations stems from energy use and carbon emissions generated by day-to-
day activities. While our influence as a bank is much greater through the financing of business activities and models, 
we remain dedicated to minimising our own operational footprint. 
We are ISO 14001-certified for Environmental Management Systems, thus ensuring continuous monitoring, updates 
and the implementation of control measures to address climate risks and opportunities in our own operations. 
Significant risks and opportunities are assigned to owners, and relevant stakeholders are actively engaged. A 
dedicated team meets monthly to discuss climate issues, with quarterly reviews focused on identifying and addressing 
new risks and opportunities. 
We have set a target for net-zero emission reductions by 2030. To achieve this, we measure, monitor and actively 
work to reduce GHG emissions across our operations. 
•Energy efficiency and renewable energy deployment in our buildings
We are upgrading all our Dutch offices to energy label A and aligning their energy efficiency with the Paris Agreement. 
By 2030, our Dutch offices will consume less than 50 kWh per square metre annually. Additionally, we are 
transitioning to 100% renewable energy in all our offices, both domestically and internationally, while working to 
reduce overall energy consumption.
•Electrification and reduction of our mobility and business travel
To decarbonise mobility, we are electrifying our lease car fleet in the Netherlands. In 2018, we joined the Anders 
Reizen Coalition, a collaboration between 70 large Dutch organisations working to reduce emissions from commuting 
and business travel.
Internationally, we are implementing policies to ensure only electric vehicle options for lease fleets. This approach is 
already in place in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany, while still pending in France and Greece. Since the electric-
lease-car-only policy has not yet been implemented in the latter two countries, new gas or diesel car contracts 
initiated in 2025 could result in vehicle emissions in 2030 if these contracts span five years. We are actively exploring 
solutions to meet our target of a fully electric international lease fleet by 2030.ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
218To decarbonise business travel, we are replacing short-distance air travel with rail travel, procuring sustainable aviation 
fuel and setting a maximum annual travel budget for each department. ABN AMRO has installed internal monitoring 
mechanisms and dashboards to allow departments to gain insight into their business travel behaviour and proactively 
steer on their maximum and remaining travel budgets. We are currently working on department-specific reduction 
plans. However, in 2023 and 2024 our business travel emissions exceeded what we strived for. Cascading travel 
budgets down to department level has not yet yielded the necessary results, but the matter has our continuous 
attention.

title: Cross-sector environmental scenario analysis
heading: 7.5.2.1 Cross-sector environmental scenario analysis
start_phrase: In 2023, ABN AMRO conducted a cross-sector environmental risk scenario analysis to assess the effects of environmental transition risks on our corporate lending clients in the Netherlands.
summary:
- Business travel decarbonisation: shift short-haul flights to rail, procure sustainable aviation fuel, and set department-level annual travel budgets. Internal dashboards enable monitoring and steering against budgets. Department-specific reduction plans are in progress, but 2023–2024 emissions exceeded targets; cascading budgets have not yet delivered desired reductions.

- Material nature topics: ESRS E2 (air and water pollution), E4 (drivers of biodiversity loss), and E5 (resource use/circular economy) are material from an impact perspective; from a risk perspective, materiality is limited to pollution.

- 2023 cross-sector environmental risk scenario analysis (Netherlands corporate lending): ABN AMRO developed a TNFD-guided, locally relevant transition-risk scenario to 2030, based on strict implementation/enforcement of EU water/air pollution and nature policies, reflecting imminent compliance deadlines, potential Dutch non-compliance, and EC intolerance for delays.

- Methodology: combined sectoral impact data (Impact Institute, Dutch Emission Registration) with geographic sensitivity data (PBL, RIVM); internalised external environmental costs to estimate financial impacts; assessed business continuity risks via assumed permitting limits for high-impact sectors in sensitive natural areas.

- Findings: water pollution-related costs and continuity risks are most significant for manufacturing and agriculture clients; management overlays applied for Dutch nitrogen-reduction policy risks.

- Forthcoming actions: integrate environmental risk into stress-testing models and finalize an Agriculture Transition Plan for the dairy sub-sector, outlining a 2040 vision, ABN AMRO’s role, and actions to support clients’ shift to sustainable and regenerative practices.
text:
Cross-sector environmental scenario analysis
In 2023, ABN AMRO conducted a cross-sector environmental risk scenario analysis to assess the effects of 
environmental transition risks on our corporate lending clients in the Netherlands. Unlike climate risk, there are no 
globally accepted environmental risk scenarios. We therefore developed our own locally relevant scenario, guided by 
the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosure (TNFD). This scenario focused on transition risk and considered a 
time horizon to 2030. 
Our scenario was based on existing European regulations and their implementation in the Netherlands. We focused on 
transition risks, which we deemed to be more relevant to our business in the short term, given the European and 
global policy context. 
The analysis assumed that European water and air pollution regulations, along with nature conservation policies, 
would be strictly implemented and enforced in the Netherlands. This assumption was based on:
•compliance deadlines: many regulations have deadlines within this timeframe
•potential non-compliance: the Netherlands may not necessarily meet these deadlines
•strict enforcement: the European Commission has signalled that further delays will not be tolerated
Using sectoral environmental impact data from the Impact Institute and the Dutch Emission Registration, along with 
geographical data from the PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency and the National Institute for Public 
Health and the Environment, we simulated the costs and business continuity risks for our clients. Costs were 
calculated by internalising the external environmental costs of pollution, while business continuity risks were 
evaluated by assuming permit limitations for clients in high-impact sectors operating in highly sensitive natural areas.
The results indicated that water pollution-related costs and business continuity risks were most significant for clients in 
the manufacturing and agriculture sectors. 
In relation to pollution risks, and specifically the Dutch government’s nitrogen-reducing measures, we have taken 
management overlays .
As we continue to update our risk management framework in relation to environmental risks, the insights from this 
scenario analysis will inform ABN AMRO’s strategic and risk management initiatives as follows: 
•Stress-testing integ ration: Work is underway to incorporate environmental risk into the bank’s stress-testing 
methodology and models.
•Agriculture Transition Plan: A transition plan for the dairy sub-sector is being drafted, outlining the bank’s vision for 
the sector in 2040. This plan will include details of ABN AMRO’s ambition and role, and an action plan to support 
clients transitioning to more sustainable and regenerative practices.ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡

Social risk heatmap
The social risk element of the environmental and social risk heatmap focuses on workers in the value chain. It 
examines the negative impacts of the sectors that our clients are active in and focuses on working conditions, equal
