title: GHG emissions for corporate loans
heading: 7.8.2.1 GHG emissions for corporate loans
start_phrase: The ISS ESG database is used as the source for collecting GHG emissions for our corporate clients.
summary:
- Focus: How ABN AMRO calculates and reports financed GHG emissions across its portfolios, aligned with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (Dec 2022).
- Methodology: Absolute emissions allocated proportional to the bank’s share of counterparty value; preference for client/collateral-level data; use of economic emission intensities when client data are unavailable.
- Data sources and methods by portfolio:
  - Corporate loans (listed bonds/equity): ISS ESG; client-reported emissions.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed, Netherlands): Statistics Netherlands (CBS) economic intensities.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed, rest of world): PCAF emission factor database.
  - Agriculture: Sector-specific factor for dairy (RVO, International Dairy Federation, research by Hospers et al. 2022); CBS intensities for other subsectors.
  - Shipping loans: Poseidon Principles and collaboration with DNV for vessel-level data; emissiefactoren.nl and KiM for inland shipping; CBS/PCAF fallbacks.
  - Oil and gas (upstream/midstream): Rystad Energy data, company disclosures, and IPCC factors; client-level carbon intensity used.
  - Power generation: BP Statistics 2022, company disclosures, Dutch government open data; client-reported plus average capacity factor estimates.
  - Road transport: TRACCS and CE Delft vehicle-type emission factors.
  - Commercial real estate: RVO and PCAF; estimates based on building type and energy label.
  - Residential mortgages: RVO, CBS, BAG; estimates based on building type, floor area, and energy label.
- Segment-specific treatments:
  - Corporate loans: ISS ESG as primary source; CBS/PCAF used when ISS coverage is missing; renewable power (solar, wind, hydro) assigned zero Scope 1 and 2; Scope 3 from client data or CBS/PCAF.
  - Agriculture: Dairy sector uses a tailored emission factor; other subsectors rely on CBS intensities.
  - Shipping: Sea/coastal freight uses Poseidon Principles/client-reported vessel data; inland shipping uses external emission factors; fallbacks to CBS/PCAF when needed.
  - Oil and gas: Portfolio intensity measured as kg CO2e per barrel produced/distributed/transported; combines client disclosures with Rystad production and intensity to establish baselines and targets.
text:
GHG emissions for corporate loans
The ISS ESG database is used as the source for collecting GHG emissions for our corporate clients. For corporate 
clients not covered by the ISS ESG database, we used the Statistics Netherlands (CBS) and PCAF databases, which 
provide country- and sector-specific carbon intensity information. For clients active in renewable energy production 
from solar power, wind power or hydropower, we used an emission intensity of 0 for scope 1 and scope 2 GHG 
emissions, as the nature of the activity already implies that no emissions are associated with these activities. For scope 
3 GHG emissions, either client-specific information was used or, if not available, the CBS and the PCAF databases were 
used.

title: GHG emissions for agriculture
heading: 7.8.2.2 GHG emissions for agriculture
start_phrase: For dairy farming, a combination of the research paper Hospers et al. (2022), RVO (via StatLine) and International Dairy Federation was used to calculate a sector-specific emission factor.
summary:
- Focus: How ABN AMRO measures and reports financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in line with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (Dec 2022).
- Core approach:
  - Absolute financed emissions are proportional to ABN AMRO’s share of exposure in a counterparty’s total value.
  - Data hierarchy prioritizes client- or collateral-level emissions; if unavailable, applies country/sector economic emission intensities.
- Portfolio-specific sources and methods:
  - Corporate loans (listed bonds/equity): ISS ESG; client-reported emissions.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed NL): Statistics Netherlands (CBS); economic emission intensity.
  - Corporate loans (non-listed RoW): PCAF emission factor database; economic emission intensity.
  - Agriculture: Dairy uses sector-specific factor (Hospers et al. 2022, RVO, International Dairy Federation); other sub-sectors use CBS intensities.
  - Shipping: Sea/coastal freight via Poseidon Principles and third-party data (e.g., DNV); inland shipping via KiM and emissiefactoren.nl; fallback to CBS/PCAF intensities.
  - Oil & Gas (upstream/midstream): Company disclosures linked with Rystad data; IPCC factors where possible; intensity measured as kg CO2e per barrel to set baselines and targets.
  - Power generation: BP Statistics 2022, company disclosures, Dutch government open databases; client-reported emissions with average capacity factor estimates when needed.
  - Road transport: TRACCS and CE Delft; external emission factors per vehicle type.
  - Commercial real estate: RVO and PCAF; estimates based on building type and energy label.
  - Residential mortgages: RVO, CBS, BAG; estimates based on building type, floor area, and energy label.
- Additional rules:
  - Renewable power producers (solar, wind, hydro) are assigned zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions; Scope 3 uses client data or CBS/PCAF where unavailable.
text:
GHG emissions for agriculture
For dairy farming, a combination of the research paper Hospers et al. (2022), RVO (via StatLine) and International Dairy 
Federation was used to calculate a sector-specific emission factor. For all other agriculture sub-sectors, we used the 
CBS database, which provides country and sector-specific carbon intensity information.

title: GHG emissions for shipping loans
heading: 7.8.2.3 GHG emissions for shipping loans
start_phrase: The Poseidon Principles framework has been used as our main source for collecting GHG emissions at vessel level for the sea and coastal freight water transport portfolio.
summary:
- Focus: How financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are calculated and reported in line with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (Dec 2022), allocating absolute emissions proportional to the bank’s share of exposure in a counterparty’s value.
- Data hierarchy: Prioritizes client or collateral-level, client-reported data; where unavailable, applies country/sector economic emission intensities and emission factors relevant to each segment.
- Portfolio methodologies and sources:
  - Corporate loans, listed bonds and equity: ISS ESG; client-reported emissions.
  - Corporate loans, non-listed Netherlands: Statistics Netherlands (CBS) economic emission intensities.
  - Corporate loans, non-listed rest of world: PCAF emission factor database.
  - Agriculture: Sector-specific emission factor for dairy using Hospers et al. (2022), RVO, International Dairy Federation; other sub-sectors via CBS intensities.
  - Shipping loans: Poseidon Principles with vessel-level data; collaboration with DNV; KiM and emissiefactoren.nl for inland shipping; fallback to CBS/PCAF for gaps.
  - Oil and gas (upstream/midstream): Rystad Energy data, company disclosures, IPCC factors; carbon intensity metric in kg CO2e per barrel produced/distributed/transported; used for baseline and targets.
  - Power generation: BP Statistics 2022, company disclosures, Dutch open government data; client-reported emissions and capacity factor estimates.
  - Road transport: TRACCS and CE Delft vehicle-type emission factors.
  - Commercial real estate: RVO and PCAF; emissions estimated from building type and energy label.
  - Residential mortgages: RVO, CBS, BAG; emissions estimated from building type, floor area, and energy label.
- Renewable energy handling: For solar, wind, and hydropower producers, scope 1 and 2 emissions set to zero; scope 3 based on client data or CBS/PCAF where unavailable.
- Overall approach: Combines multiple databases and sector-specific methodologies to estimate financed emissions consistently across asset classes.
text:
GHG emissions for shipping loans
The Poseidon Principles framework has been used as our main source for collecting GHG emissions at vessel level for 
the sea and coastal freight water transport portfolio. ABN AMRO also collaborates with third-party providers like DNV 
to collect, review, process the data and calculate the performance of the vessels in our portfolio. The Kennisinstituut 
voor Mobiliteitsbeleid (KiM) and emissiefactoren.nl database was used as a source to collect GHG emissions for inland 
shipping cargo vessels. For all vessels not covered by the above-mentioned sources, we used the CBS and the PCAF 
databases, which provide country and sector-specific carbon intensity information.

title: GHG emissions for oil and gas - upstream and midstream
heading: 7.8.2.4 GHG emissions for oil and gas - upstream and midstream
start_phrase: For the ABN AMRO portfolio, the carbon intensity metric measures the kg of CO 2e emissions for each barrel of oil produced, distributed or transported by each client we finance.
summary:
- Purpose and framework: Describes how financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are measured in line with the PCAF Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard (Dec 2022), attributing absolute emissions proportionally to the bank’s share of exposure in a counterparty’s value.
- Data hierarchy and approach: Prioritizes client- or collateral-level data; otherwise applies economic/sectoral emission intensities. Summarizes key data sources and methods per portfolio segment.
- Portfolio methodologies and sources:
  - Corporate loans (listed, bonds, equity): ISS ESG client-reported emissions. For non-listed NL clients: Statistics Netherlands (CBS) intensities; Rest of world: PCAF emission factor database. Renewable power producers assigned zero scope 1–2; scope 3 from client data or CBS/PCAF.
  - Agriculture: Dairy farming uses a sector-specific factor (Hospers et al. 2022, RVO, International Dairy Federation). Other sub-sectors use CBS country/sector intensities.
  - Shipping: Sea/coastal freight uses Poseidon Principles and third-party validation (e.g., DNV) with vessel-level data; inland shipping uses KiM and emissiefactoren.nl. Fallback: CBS/PCAF.
  - Oil & gas (upstream/midstream): Carbon intensity in kg CO2e per barrel using Rystad Energy, company disclosures; IPCC factors for combustion; proxies where data is missing.
  - Power generation: Company disclosures, BP Energy Statistics 2022, Dutch government open data (overheid.nl), and internal databases; estimates used to close gaps (e.g., average capacity factors).
  - Road transport: Trucks measured in gCO2/tonne-km; vans in gCO2/vehicle-km (scope 1), with scope 2 from electricity use. TRACCS provides activity data and emission factors (UK, DE); CE Delft for NL. Passenger cars use external emission factors, average distances, and grid-intensity-based scope 2.
  - Commercial real estate: Scope 1–2 based on energy label and asset type with PCAF emission factors.
  - Residential mortgages: PCAF-aligned method using building type, floor area, and energy label; CBS energy consumption and emission factors; loan-level attribution by gross carrying amount to property value at origination.
- Scope 3 reporting: As of 31 Dec 2023, upstream scope 3 estimated via PCAF EEIO emission factors; lowest data quality score noted.
- Company-specific reporting coverage: Defined as the share of gross carrying amount calculated with PCAF data quality scores 1–3 (company-specific inputs).
- Maturity treatment: Exposures without stated maturity and borrower-determined repayment are placed in a 20-year bucket; weighted average maturity estimated from bucket averages.
text:
GHG emissions for oil and gas - upstream and midstream
For the ABN AMRO portfolio, the carbon intensity metric measures the kg of CO 2e emissions for each barrel of oil 
produced, distributed or transported by each client we finance. ABN AMRO links client data (company specific 
disclosures) to carbon intensity and production data from Rystad to calculate the carbon intensity baseline and target. ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
245IPCC was used for emissions factors related to combustion of fossil fuels. Appropriate proxies are used in instances 
where carbon intensity and production data are not available.

title: GHG emissions for power generation
heading: 7.8.2.5 GHG emissions for power generation
start_phrase: For power generation, a combination of company disclosures, BP energy statistics 2022 and an internal database was used.
summary:
- Methodology for calculating financed GHG emissions across sectors, with IPCC emission factors for fossil fuel combustion and use of proxies where carbon intensity/production data are missing.
- Power generation: emissions estimated using a mix of company disclosures, BP Energy Statistics 2022, and an internal database; data gaps bridged with estimates including average capacity factors from BP 2022.
- Road transport: financed emissions calculated for trucks (g CO2 per tonne-km) and vans (g CO2 per vehicle-km) for scope 1; scope 2 based on electricity consumption. TRACCS used for vehicle activity data and emission factors (UK, Germany), CE Delft for the Netherlands. Passenger cars rely on external emission factors, average distances, electricity consumption, and grid intensity for scopes 1 and 2.
- Real estate: residential mortgage emissions per PCAF standard using floor area, energy labels, and asset type; CBS energy consumption and emission factors applied; loan-level attribution based on gross carrying amount to property value at origination. Commercial real estate scope 1 and 2 emissions based on energy label and asset type using PCAF emission factor database.
- Scope 3: reporting client scope 3 estimates as of 31 Dec 2023 using PCAF EEIO industry carbon intensities; acknowledges lowest data quality and coverage limited to upstream scope 3.
- Data quality and portfolio coverage: “Percentage of portfolio derived from company-specific reporting” defined as share of gross carrying amount with PCAF data quality scores 1–3.
- Maturity treatment: exposures without stated maturity and with borrower-determined repayment classified in a 20-year bucket; average weighted maturity estimated from bucket averages.
text:
GHG emissions for power generation
For power generation, a combination of company disclosures, BP energy statistics 2022 and an internal database was 
used. Most of the emissions data used to measure and track our clients’ emissions, was a combination of internal and 
public company disclosures. Wherever possible, data gaps were addressed using estimates, at times with external 
guidance, such as the average capacity factor of different sources of power generation in Europe taken from BP 
Energy Statistics 2022.

title: GHG emissions for road transport
heading: 7.8.2.6 GHG emissions for road transport
start_phrase: We measure our financed emissions for trucks in grams of CO 2 associated with each transported tonne of freight per kilometre and our financed emissions for vans in grams of CO 2 per vehicle kilometre capturing the scope 1 GHG emissions.
summary:
- Emission factor methodology: IPCC factors used for fossil fuel combustion; proxies applied when carbon intensity or production data are unavailable.
- Power generation: Emissions estimated using company disclosures, BP Energy Statistics 2022, and an internal database; data gaps filled with estimates (e.g., European capacity factors from BP 2022).
- Road transport: Financed emissions measured as grams CO2/tonne-km for trucks and grams CO2/vehicle-km for vans (scope 1), with scope 2 based on electricity use; TRACCS used for vehicle activity and emission factors (UK, Germany), CE Delft for Dutch factors; passenger cars use external emission factors and travel distances for scope 1, and electricity consumption plus grid intensity for scope 2.
- Residential mortgages: Calculations align with PCAF, based on floor area, energy labels, and asset type; CBS energy consumption and emission factors used; loan-level attribution factor applied (gross carrying amount/property value at origination).
- Commercial real estate: Scope 1 and 2 emissions based on energy label and asset type using PCAF emission factor database.
- Scope 3: As of 31 Dec 2023, estimates rely on PCAF EEIO carbon intensities by industry; lowest data quality score; limited to upstream scope 3 only.
- Company-specific reporting share: Defined as the percentage of gross carrying amount calculated with PCAF data quality scores 1–3 (company-specific inputs).
- Maturity buckets: Exposures without stated maturity and with counterparty-determined repayment dates placed in a 20-year bucket; average weighted maturity estimated from bucket averages.
text:
GHG emissions for road transport
We measure our financed emissions for trucks in grams of CO 2 associated with each transported tonne of freight per 
kilometre and our financed emissions for vans in grams of CO 2 per vehicle kilometre capturing the scope 1 GHG 
emissions. The scope 2 emissions for trucks and vans are calculated based on electricity consumption. TRACCS was 
used for vehicle activity for all countries and for emissions factors for the UK and Germany, while CE Delft was used for 
emissions factors for the Netherlands. For passenger cars, we rely on external emission factors, as well as average 
distances travelled, to calculate the financed scope 1 emissions associated with our portfolio, and we rely on external 
data on electricity consumption, as well as electricity grid intensity, to calculate the scope 2 emissions financed.

title: GHG emissions for commercial real estate and residential mortgages
heading: 7.8.2.7 GHG emissions for commercial real estate and residential mortgages
start_phrase: For residential mortgages, the calculations are in line with the PCAF standard and based on floor area, energy labels and asset type.
summary:
- Methodological framework for financed emissions, using IPCC combustion emission factors and proxies where carbon intensity or production data are unavailable.
- Power generation: emissions estimated from a mix of company disclosures, BP Energy Statistics 2022, and internal databases; data gaps filled with estimates (e.g., average capacity factors from BP).
- Road transport: scope 1 and 2 financed emissions calculated for trucks, vans, and passenger cars.
  - Trucks: grams CO2 per tonne-kilometre; vans: grams CO2 per vehicle-kilometre; scope 2 based on electricity consumption.
  - Data sources include TRACCS for vehicle activity (all countries) and emission factors (UK, Germany), CE Delft for Netherlands factors; passenger cars use external emission factors, average distances, electricity consumption, and grid intensity.
- Residential mortgages: PCAF-aligned approach using floor area, energy labels, and asset type; CBS energy data and emission factors to convert energy to CO2; loan-level attribution factor based on gross carrying amount vs. property value at origination.
- Commercial real estate: scope 1 and 2 based on energy label and asset type with PCAF emission factor database.
- Scope 3: reporting estimated upstream scope 3 using PCAF EEIO industry carbon intensities; noted as lowest data quality and limited to upstream emissions.
- Definition of “percentage of portfolio from company-specific reporting”: share of gross carrying amount calculated with PCAF data quality scores 1–3.
- Maturity treatment: exposures without stated maturity placed in a 20-year bucket; average weighted maturity estimated using the average of each maturity bucket.
text:
GHG emissions for commercial real estate and residential mortgages
For residential mortgages, the calculations are in line with the PCAF standard and based on floor area, energy labels 
and asset type. CBS data for energy consumption has been used to calculate CO 2 emissions. To convert the energy 
data into carbon emission data, the emission factors provided by CBS were used. An attribution factor at loan level has 
been applied; this is the ratio of the gross carrying amount and the property value at origination.
For the commercial real estate financing portfolio, the GHG emissions calculations (scope 1 and 2) are based on 
energy label and asset type, and the corresponding emission factors provided by the PCAF emission factor database.

title: Scope 3 emissions
heading: 7.8.2.8 Scope 3 emissions
start_phrase: As of 31 December 2023, we are reporting estimates of our clients’ scope 3 emissions.
summary:
- Describes methodologies and data sources for calculating financed GHG emissions across sectors, using IPCC emission factors for fossil fuel combustion and proxies where carbon intensity or production data are missing.
- Power generation: Emissions estimated from a mix of company disclosures, BP Energy Statistics 2022, and internal databases; data gaps addressed with estimates such as average capacity factors from BP.
- Road transport: Financed emissions for trucks measured in gCO2 per tonne-km and for vans in gCO2 per vehicle-km (scope 1), with scope 2 based on electricity consumption; TRACCS provides activity data and emission factors (UK, Germany), CE Delft for the Netherlands; passenger car emissions use external factors and average distances, and scope 2 from electricity consumption and grid intensity.
- Residential mortgages: Calculations align with PCAF, using floor area, energy labels, asset type; CBS energy consumption and emission factors convert to CO2; loan-level attribution factor based on gross carrying amount versus property value at origination.
- Commercial real estate: Scope 1 and 2 emissions based on energy labels and asset type using PCAF emission factor database.
- Scope 3: As of 31 Dec 2023, reports estimated upstream scope 3 emissions using PCAF EEIO carbon intensity factors, acknowledged as lowest data quality.
- Defines “percentage of portfolio from company-specific reporting” as the share of gross carrying amount tied to emissions calculated with PCAF data quality scores 1–3.
- Maturity methodology: Exposures without stated maturity and callable by counterparties placed in a 20-year bucket; average weighted maturity estimated from bucket averages.
text:
Scope 3 emissions
As of 31 December 2023, we are reporting estimates of our clients’ scope 3 emissions. They depend entirely on the 
environmentally extended input-output (EEIO) emission factors carbon intensities by industry as supplied by the PCAF. 
These emission factors have the lowest data quality score and are currently limited to upstream scope 3 GHG 
emissions only.

title: ESG2 - Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Loans collateralised by immovable property - Energy efficiency of the collateral
heading: 7.9 ESG2 - Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Loans collateralised by immovable property - Energy efficiency of the collateral
start_phrase: Specifically for loans collateralised by residential immovable property, the amounts attributed to EPC labels in this report consist of EPC labels under the old regulation (NEN7120, prior to 1 January 2021) and new regulation (NTA8800) as provided by Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland (RVO).
summary:
- Scope and purpose: ESG2 disclosure on climate change transition risk for ABN AMRO’s banking book, focusing on the energy efficiency of collateral for loans secured by immovable property (residential and commercial) using EP scores (kWh/m²) and EPC labels.
- Methodology and data sources:
  - Residential EPC labels include both old regulation (NEN7120, pre-2021) and new regulation (NTA8800) as provided by RVO.
  - Only the new regulation EP score is “official” in EP score columns; old-regulation EP scores are treated as estimated.
  - EP score columns (B–G) combine official and estimated values; EPC label columns (H–N) include only official labels.
  - Exposures without an official EPC label are reported under “Without EPC label of collateral,” including buildings exempt from labels (e.g., monuments), assets under development/not yet registered, and cases where the label is unknown to the bank.
- Portfolio strategy and progress:
  - ABN AMRO targets lower portfolio emissions by increasing A and higher-than-A labels and reducing exposure to D–G labels.
  - From 30 June 2024 to 31 December 2024, official energy labels increased from 52% to 55%; 76% of the portfolio had a label of C or higher (vs 74% on 30 June 2024).
  - Growth in A and higher-than-A driven by new inflow (labels mandatory at sale/purchase) and migration from lower-than-A; new-build homes under the Building Decree have at least A+++.
- Key figures at 31 December 2024 (EU area):
  - Total gross carrying amount: EUR 185.95bn (Commercial: EUR 26.77bn; Residential: EUR 159.19bn).
  - EP score distribution concentrated in ≤200 kWh/m²: EUR 55.85bn (0–100) and EUR 91.67bn (>100–200).
  - A large share of EP scores are estimated: EUR 130.93bn of the EU-area total is based on estimated EP scores.
  - Official EPC labels (A includes >A): A EUR 44.92bn, B EUR 13.05bn, C EUR 18.87bn, D EUR 9.09bn, E EUR 6.06bn, F EUR 4.85bn, G EUR 4.93bn; “Without EPC label of collateral”: EUR 84.20bn.
- Non-EU exposures are minimal (EUR 0.18bn total at 31 December 2024).
- Repossessed collateral: none at 31 December 2024 (no exposures related to repossessed residential or commercial properties).
- Comparative context (30 June 2024 and 31 December 2023 tables provided): show stable EP score banding, rising share of official labels, and improving distribution toward higher energy efficiency over time.
text:
ESG2 - Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Loans collateralised by immovable 
property - Energy efficiency of the collateral
Specifically for loans collateralised by residential immovable property, the amounts attributed to EPC labels in this 
report consist of EPC labels under the old regulation (NEN7120, prior to 1 January 2021) and new regulation 
(NTA8800) as provided by Rijksdienst voor Ondernemend Nederland (RVO). While both old and new regulation EPC 
labels are considered ‘official’ in column H-N, only the new regulation EP score is considered ‘official’ in column B-G. 
The new regulation EPC label is provided with an accompanying EP score, while this is not the case for the old 
regulation EPC label where EP score is classified as estimated in column B-G.
As such, the attribution of gross carrying amounts to the EP score in row 5 column A subsequently columns B-G, are
higher than the gross carrying amounts of the estimated EPC labels in row 1 column P-O.
For all loans collateralised by immovable property, in accordance with the instruction, the columns that show the EP 
score include official as well as estimated labels, while the columns that show the EPC labels only include official 
energy labels. All the exposures without an official EPC label are reported in the column 'Without EPC label of 
collateral'. This includes estimated energy labels for:
• buildings that are not required to have an energy label under the Regulation (“no label”), such as monuments
• buildings that are under development or net yet registered, for which the label cannot be estimated (“unknown 
label”)
• buildings whose energy label is not known to ABN AMRO due to other reasons
As part of its climate strategy, ABN AMRO has set targets to reduce its carbon footprint. ABN AMRO continues to work 
towards this goal by seeking to increase the A and higher-than-A-labels and lowering the exposure to D-G energy 
labels. In line with this strategy, the distribution of official energy labels showed a slight improvement compared to Q2 
2024, with an increase in official energy labels from 52% to 55%, the majority being A labels and 76% of the portfolio 
having an energy label of C or higher (30 June 2024: 74%).
The increase in the category official EPC label A and higher-than-A labels was partly a result of new inflow and 
migration from the lower-than-A labels to label A. New inflow usually has an official energy label, given that such a 
label is mandatory at the time of a sale or purchase transaction. In addition, new-build houses based on the Building 
Decree (Besluit Bouwwerken Leefomgeving) have at least an A+++ label.

title: ESG3 – Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Alignment metrics - Introduction
heading: 7.10 ESG3 – Banking book - Climate change transition risk: Alignment metrics
start_phrase: T h i s t e m p l a t e a i m s t o c a p t u r e t h e b a n k ’ s a l i g n m e n t e f f o r t s w i t h r e s p e c t t o t h e o b j e c t i v e s o f t h e P a r i s A g r e e m e n t f o r a s e l e c t e d n u m b e r o f s e c t o r s .
summary: Introduces Template 3 for banking-book climate transition risk alignment metrics, outlining how ABN AMRO reports sector-based alignment with Paris Agreement objectives consistent with its climate strategy as disclosed in the Integrated Annual Report (IAR). It explains that sectors and NACE codes in Template 3 match the bank’s strategy, with targets prioritizing carbon‑intensive sectors per NZBA and focusing on the most material value chain segments. Scope differences are highlighted: the EBA template covers non‑financial counterparties, while ABN AMRO’s strategy covers all counterparties, causing discrepancies in gross carrying amounts and emission intensities between the IAR and Pillar 3, notably in agriculture where many exposures are classified as households (outside the template), making Template 3 intensities lower and even below target. Product coverage aligns with the climate strategy and currently excludes debt securities and equity instruments; future inclusion would be reflected in Template 3. The decarbonization benchmark follows the IEA NZE2050 scenario, while ABN AMRO applies sector‑specific scenarios for shipping, commercial real estate, and agriculture.

title: Power generation
heading: 7.10.1 Power generation
start_phrase: Data reported directly by our clients is used to calculate the emissions intensity of the power generation portfolio.
summary:
- Purpose: Presents ESG3 Template 3 alignment metrics for ABN AMRO’s banking book, showing progress toward Paris Agreement objectives across selected, climate‑material sectors aligned with the bank’s climate strategy and primarily disclosed in the Integrated Annual Report (IAR).
- Approach: Sector-based target setting prioritising carbon‑intensive sectors per NZBA; focuses on the most material parts of each value chain. Sectors and NACE codes in Template 3 mirror those in the climate strategy.
- Scope differences: EBA template covers non‑financial counterparties, while ABN AMRO’s strategy covers all counterparties. This creates discrepancies in gross carrying amounts and intensities versus the IAR—most notably in agriculture, where a large household share is out of scope, lowering Template 3 intensities (even below target) relative to strategy targets based on full scope.
- Product coverage: Template 3 includes products aligned with the climate strategy; debt securities and equity instruments are currently excluded but may be added if brought into scope in future.
- Scenarios: Uses IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE2050) pathway as EBA benchmark; ABN AMRO applies sector‑specific scenarios for shipping, commercial real estate, and agriculture.
- Data and timing: Emissions intensities are derived from client‑reported data with a one‑year reporting lag for consistency.
- Sector metrics:
  - Power generation: Q4 2024 portfolio emissions intensity 3.5 kgCO2/MWh; below 2030 target; distance to IEA NZE2050 scenario 0%.
  - Fossil fuel combustion – oil and gas upstream: 2024 commitments EUR 804 million; below 2030 target; distance to NZE2050 0%.
  - Oil and gas upstream and midstream: Target to be first published in the 2024 IAR; target‑driving processes just initiated; operational intensity figures reported with a one‑year lag; methodology detailed in the IAR.
- Forward look: Additional sectors brought into the climate strategy will be incorporated into Template 3 accordingly.

- Power generation: Emissions intensity is based on client-reported data with a one-year reporting lag. As of Q4 2024, intensity was 3.5 kgCO2/MWh, below the 2030 target; distance to the IEA NZE2050 scenario is 0%.

- Oil and gas upstream and midstream: Targeting begins with publication in the 2024 IAR; operational emission intensity reported with a one-year delay; methodology details are in the IAR.

title: Oil and gas upstream and midstream
heading: 7.10.3 Oil and gas upstream and midstream
start_phrase: Since our target for oil and gas upstream and midstream will be first published in the 2024 Integrated Annual Report, the processes to actively drive the target have only just begun.
summary:
- Purpose and scope: ESG3 template reports ABN AMRO’s portfolio alignment with Paris Agreement objectives for selected, climate‑material sectors, aligned with the bank’s climate strategy as primarily disclosed in the Integrated Annual Report (IAR). Targets are set by sector, prioritizing carbon‑intensive activities per NZBA, and focusing on the most material parts of each value chain. Sectors and NACE codes shown mirror those in the bank’s climate strategy.
- Counterparty and product coverage: EBA Template 3 focuses on non‑financial counterparties, while ABN AMRO’s strategy covers all counterparties, creating discrepancies versus the IAR—most notably in agriculture, where a large share classified as households is excluded here, lowering reported emission intensity below the strategy target. Products included match the climate strategy; debt securities and equity instruments are currently out of scope but may be added in future.
- Scenario references: EBA requires IEA NZE2050 sectoral pathways. ABN AMRO uses sector‑specific scenarios for shipping, commercial real estate (CRE), and agriculture.
- Data timing: Several sector intensities are reported with a one‑year lag to ensure consistent client‑reported datasets.
- Power generation: Client‑reported data; Q4 2024 emissions intensity of 3.5 kgCO2/MWh, below the 2030 target; distance to IEA NZE2050 scenario is 0%.
- Fossil fuel combustion – oil and gas upstream: 2024 commitments reduced to EUR 804 million, well below the 2030 target; distance to NZE2050 is 0%. Upstream and midstream targets to be first published in the 2024 IAR; methodologies and operational intensity figures use a one‑year lag.
- Automotive:
  - Trucks and vans (asset‑based financing lease portfolio): Trucks intensity 79.8 gCO2/tkm; 31% distance to NZE2050. Vans intensity 218.6 gCO2/vkm; 55% distance to NZE2050.
  - Passenger cars (direct lease and ALFAM consumer loans): Target first published in 2024 IAR; processes initiated; figures use 31 Dec 2023 as base year; methodology in IAR.
- Maritime transport:
  - Deep sea shipping: Uses verified Poseidon Principles data with a one‑year lag. In 2024 adopted DNV 1.5°C trajectory (Scenario 10); alignment delta −2%; target is full alignment with DNV 1.5°C.
  - Inland freight water: Q4 2024 intensity 25.1 gCO2/tkm (improved from 26.6 in Q2). Metric based on average by ship size. Due to lack of a dedicated benchmark, the IEA freight and shipping benchmark (aggregating maritime and trucking) is applied, implying a low baseline.
- Agriculture: Baseline and 2030 targets use Dutch national averages. Pillar 3 counterparty scope excludes household exposures, reducing financed emissions and showing an alignment metric lower than the bank’s target.
- Commercial real estate (CRE): Q4 2024 intensity 58.2 kgCO2/m2 (down from 61.9 in Q2), driven by a higher share of A‑or‑better energy labels and fewer D–G labels.
- Forward scope changes: Additional sectors/products added to the bank’s climate strategy will be incorporated into Template 3 in future reporting.

Inland freight water
For inland freight water transport (inland shipping) the intensity metric for Q4 2024 was 25.1 gCO 2/tkm, and is a slight

title: ESG5 - Banking book - Climate change physical risk: Exposures subject to physical risk - Introduction
heading: 7.12 ESG5 - Banking book - Climate change physical risk: Exposures subject to physical risk
start_phrase: Physical risk in the context of this template refers to the financial impact of a changing climate.
summary: Introduces ABN AMRO’s ESG5 disclosure on banking book exposures subject to climate change physical risk, defining physical risk (acute from extreme events vs chronic from progressive shifts) and scoping out environmental degradation (pollution, biodiversity loss, deforestation). The assessment covers six hazards—flooding, heat stress, hurricanes & typhoons, sea level rise, water stress, wildfires—plus buildings’ foundational risk due to drought; chronic risks are heat stress, water stress, and foundational risks, while acute risks are flooding, hurricanes & typhoons, wildfires, and sea level rise. Versus 30 June 2024, exposures sensitive to physical risk rose slightly mainly due to a mortgage methodology update, while total exposure declined slightly. Most exposure is in the Netherlands, with urban West (Amsterdam, Rotterdam) showing lower sensitivity due to strong flood protection, some flood risk near rivers, and higher chronic risk sensitivity in agriculture concentrated in the North and East. Detailed tables (31 Dec 2024, 30 Jun 2024, 31 Dec 2023) provide sector-level gross carrying amounts; portions sensitive to physical risk (chronic, acute, and both); maturity buckets and average weighted maturity; Stage 2 and non‑performing exposures; and accumulated impairments/provisions, including lines for residential and commercial real estate loans.
text:
ESG5 - Banking book - Climate change physical risk: Exposures subject to physical risk
Physical risk in the context of this template refers to the financial impact of a changing climate. It is categorised as 
“acute” when it arises from extreme events, such as droughts, floods and storms, and “chronic” when it arises from 
progressive shifts, such as increasing temperatures and water stress. While impact from environmental degradation, 
such as air, water and land pollution, biodiversity loss and deforestation also qualifies as physical risk, it is not in scope 
of this disclosure. This report’s physical risk assessment considers six climate hazards (flooding, heat stress, hurricanes 
& typhoons, sea level rise, water stress and wildfires) in addition to buildings’ foundational risk due to drought. The 
hazards linked to chronic risk are heat stress, water stress, and foundational risks, while those linked to acute risk are 
flooding, hurricanes & typhoons, wildfires and sea level rise.
Compared to 30 June 2024, our exposure sensitive to impact from climate change events increased slightly, mainly 
due to methodology update for mortgages, while the total exposure decreased slightly. The majority of our portfolio is 
located in the Netherlands, which has varying degrees of sensitivity to the impact of flooding, sea level rise and water 
stress. Most of the Dutch collateral and counterparties in our portfolio are located in the Western part of the country, 
some of which are sensitive to flood risk depending on the proximity to rivers. The majority of our exposures in the 
West are in urban areas around Amsterdam and Rotterdam, which have lower sensitivity to physical risk, also because 
of the highly developed flood protection systems in these cities. The agriculture sector has a large share of exposure in 
the North and East relative to other sectors in our portfolio, resulting in higher sensitivity to chronic risk. 
The next sections contain more details on the data sources and methodology used to arrive at the disclosed figures.ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡

title: Methodology and Data Sources
heading: 7.12.1 Methodology and Data Sources
start_phrase: Physical risk is categorised as acute when it arises from extreme events, such as droughts, floods, and storms.
summary:
- Defines physical climate risk categories: acute (extreme events like droughts, floods, storms) and chronic (progressive shifts like rising temperatures, water stress, biodiversity loss, resource scarcity).
- Explains exposure assessment based on counterparty and collateral location plus sector of activity, using two data layers: geographic hazard data and sector sensitivities.
- Details geographic hazard data sources by asset type and location:
  - Netherlands, residential real estate collateral: Climate Impact Atlas (flooding, wildfires) and Kennis Centrum Aanpak Funderingsproblematiek for foundation risks.
  - Netherlands, commercial or unsecured: Climate Impact Atlas (flooding); Moody’s ESG Solutions for wildfires, heat stress, water stress, hurricanes/typhoons, sea level rise.
  - Outside the Netherlands: Moody’s ESG Solutions for flooding, wildfires, heat stress, water stress, hurricanes/typhoons, sea level rise.
- Highlights foundation problems as a key physical risk driver in Dutch real estate.
- Sources sector sensitivities from the Environmental and Social Risk Heatmap at NACE level 4 (e.g., flood sensitivity via dependence on physical assets; water stress via water dependence).
- Describes methodology: start with climate hazard exposure at counterparty/collateral location; mark sensitivity to acute or chronic risk per Moody’s ESG Solutions; apply a specific Dutch flooding rule—classify as acute if ≥10% of buildings in the NUTS region face >0.5 m flooding.
- Presents ESG6 GAR KPI coverage snapshots:
  - As of 31 Dec 2024: GAR stock—11% climate change mitigation, 0% adaptation, 11% total; 80% coverage over total assets. GAR flow—23% mitigation, 0% adaptation, 23% total; note that % coverage over total assets for flow is not feasible due to template limitations.
  - As of 30 Jun 2024: GAR stock—9% mitigation, 0% adaptation, 9% total; 81% coverage. GAR flow left blank, with reporting to start in Q4 2024.
- Notes a methodological change affecting coverage percentages: updated formula compares covered assets with total assets (vs. prior alignment-to-total-assets approach), per new guidance.
text:
Methodology and Data Sources 
Physical risk is categorised as acute when it arises from extreme events, such as droughts, floods, and storms. Physical 
risk is categorised as chronic when it arises from progressive shifts, such as increasing temperatures, water stress, 
biodiversity loss, and resource scarcity. The assessment of whether there is exposures to physical risk takes into 
account the location of counter parties and collateral, and the sector in which the counterparty operates. There are 
two layers of data: i) geographic physical risk data, and ii) sectors sensitivities for physical risk. Geographic physical risk 
data comes from: i) locations in the Netherlands collateralised by residential real estate, which contains information on 
flooding and wildfires from the Climate Impact Atlas (CIA) and information on foundation risks from the Kennis 
Centrum Aanpak Funderingsproblematiek; ii) other locations in the Netherlands, which includes flooding data from the 
CIA and information on wildfires, heat stress, water stress, hurricanes and typhoons and sea level rise from Moody's; iii) 
locations outside the Netherlands, which includes information on flooding, wildfires, heat stress, water stress, 
hurricanes and typhoons and sea level rise from Moody's. Foundation problems are an important driver of physical 
climate risk in the Dutch real estate sector. Sector sensitivities for physical risk are obtained from the Environmental 
and Social Risk Heatmap and are at NACE level 4. Examples of sector sensitivities include assessing flooding sensitivity 
based on dependency on physical assets and evaluating water stress sensitivity based on water dependence.

The starting point of the physical risk assessment is the climate hazard exposure to a counterparty’s geographical 
location or, when available, its collateral. The exposure is marked as sensitive to acute or chronic risk if the location is  
sensitive to one of the underlying hazards, as in Moody’s ESG Solutions methodology. An alternative approach is used 
for Dutch flooding events: a Dutch exposure is classified as sensitive to acute risk if at least 10% of buildings in the 
NUTS region are exposed to flooding of more than half a metre.

heading: 7.13 ESG6 - Summary of GAR KPIs
start_phrase: The table requests the percentage of coverage over total assets for stock and flow.
summary:
- Defines physical climate risk categories: acute (extreme events like droughts, floods, storms) and chronic (progressive shifts like rising temperatures, water stress, biodiversity loss, resource scarcity).
- Outlines a two-layer assessment approach combining:
  - Geographic physical risk data (by counterparty/collateral location).
  - Sector sensitivities to physical risk (NACE level 4 via the Environmental and Social Risk Heatmap), with examples such as flood sensitivity driven by reliance on physical assets and water stress sensitivity based on water dependence.
- Details data sources by geography/asset type and hazard:
  - Netherlands, residential real estate collateral: Climate Impact Atlas (flooding, wildfires) and Kennis Centrum Aanpak Funderingsproblematiek (foundation risks).
  - Netherlands, other loans/collateral: CIA (flooding) and Moody’s ESG Solutions (wildfires, heat stress, water stress, hurricanes/typhoons, sea level rise).
  - Outside the Netherlands: Moody’s ESG Solutions (flooding, wildfires, heat stress, water stress, hurricanes/typhoons, sea level rise).
  - Notes foundation problems as a key driver of physical climate risk in Dutch real estate.
- Describes exposure classification:
  - Starts from climate hazard exposure at the counterparty’s or collateral’s location.
  - Marks sensitivity to acute/chronic risk per Moody’s ESG Solutions methodology if sensitive to any underlying hazard.
  - Uses an alternative Dutch flooding rule: classify as acute-risk sensitive if at least 10% of buildings in the NUTS region face >0.5 m flooding.

title: Mitigating actions: Assets for the calculation of GAR
heading: 7.14 ESG7 - Mitigating actions: Assets for the calculation of GAR
start_phrase: As there is no line item in the P3 template for exposures towards non-NFRD financial corporations, these exposures are included in the line item 'other assets'.
summary:
- Focus: EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures from ABN AMRO’s Pillar 3 Report 2024, covering KPI scope, methodology, and detailed breakdowns for 31 Dec 2023, 30 Jun 2024, and 31 Dec 2024.
- KPI coverage and timing:
  - KPI% coverage over total assets (Dec-2023) shows circa 10% coverage for climate change mitigation; climate adaptation coverage was 0% at that time.
  - GAR “flow” metrics are left blank; reporting will start from Q4 2024 to align with the Integrated Annual Report 2024 approach.
- GAR composition and methodology:
  - Detailed allocation of assets between numerator and denominator per EU Taxonomy rules, with explicit categories:
    - Included in numerator and denominator: loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds), and equity not held for trading.
    - Excluded from numerator but included in denominator: EU and non-EU non-financial corporates not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans, cash, and other assets.
    - Excluded from both numerator and denominator: sovereigns, central bank exposures, and trading book positions.
  - Reconciliation note: Because the Pillar 3 template lacks a line for non-NFRD financial corporations, these are shown under “other assets” to reconcile FINREP and EU Taxonomy definitions.
- Asset class breakdowns:
  - Financial corporations: split into credit institutions, other financial corporations (including investment firms and management companies), and insurance undertakings; instruments split into loans, debt securities (incl. UoP), and equity.
  - Non-financial corporations subject to NFRD: reported with taxonomy-eligible and aligned amounts.
  - Households: major share of GAR assets, driven by mortgages (loans collateralised by residential property), renovation loans, and motor vehicle loans; collateral obtained by possession is also shown.
- Climate objectives and sub-categories:
  - Both Climate Change Mitigation (CCM) and Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) are reported, including “specialised lending,” “transitional,” and “enabling” categories where applicable.
- Key quantitative highlights (illustrative from the period tables):
  - Total assets and GAR denominators:
    - Dec-2023: total assets ~390bn; GAR denominator ~305bn (with ~85bn excluded: sovereigns, central banks, trading).
    - Jun-2024: total assets ~406bn; GAR denominator ~328bn (with ~78bn excluded).
    - Dec-2024: total assets ~395bn; GAR denominator ~315bn (with ~79bn excluded).
  - Households dominate GAR-covered assets; mortgages represent the bulk (circa 155–158bn across periods).
  - Taxonomy eligibility and alignment (Dec-2024 ESG8 KPIs on stock):
    - Within covered assets: CCM-eligible ≈ 52%, of which ≈ 11% aligned; CCA-eligible ≈ 50%.
    - Households: 100% CCM-eligible; a material portion (about 22%) is CCM-aligned; household mortgages and renovation loans are now also assessed under CCA.
- Methodological updates and clarifications:
  - Household activities: CCM eligibility is used as the primary measure to capture all household-related eligibility (including items that would also be eligible under CCA and Circular Economy) to avoid double counting.
  - Regulatory update: building renovation loans and loans collateralised by residential property are newly included under CCA in 2024 due to EU Taxonomy scope expansion.
text:
As there is no line item in the P3 template for exposures towards non-NFRD financial corporations, these exposures are included in the line item 'other assets'. The necessity 
for this is to reconcile with the EU Taxonomy where non-NFRD financial corporations are included in the disclosures as a separate line item.  In order to reconcile with the EU 
Taxonomy disclosures, in the total 'Other financial corporations', exposures to financial corporations that are defined as such under the FINREP but are non-financial under EU 
Taxonomy, are taking into account. This additional category was created in the EU Taxonomy template to remain aligned with the finrep definition of a financial corporation 
while simultaneously remain in compliance with the EUT. 
2. For household-related activities, the approach taken uses Climate Change Mitigation (CCM) eligibility as the primary measure of total eligibility. CCM encompasses the full 
scope of eligibility related to households, effectively capturing activities that are also eligible under Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) and Circular Economy (CE). This 
approach ensures a more precise depiction of eligibility and avoids double counting. 
3. The household product loans collateralised by rip and renovation loans have been included in this year's assessment for Climate Change Adaptation, these were previously 
not in scope for this environmental objective. This change aligns with the recent update to the EU Taxonomy regulation, which has expanded the scope of these household 
products to include not only Climate Change Mitigation (CCM) but also Climate Change Adaptation (CCA).A B C D E F G H I J K

start_phrase: As there is no line item in the P3 template for exposures towards non-NFRD financial corporations, these exposures are included in the line item 'other assets'.
summary:
- Purpose and scope: The excerpt presents ABN AMRO’s EU Taxonomy-aligned Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures (ESG8) and a supplementary disclosure on other climate-mitigating actions (ESG10) from the Pillar 3 Report 2024. It covers key performance indicators (KPIs) on both stock and flow bases for Climate Change Mitigation (CCM) and Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) across multiple reporting dates (31 Dec 2023, 30 Jun 2024, 31 Dec 2024).

- GAR KPIs on stock:
  - Measures the proportion of eligible assets funding taxonomy-relevant sectors and, within that, the share that is environmentally sustainable.
  - Breakdowns by counterparty segments: financial corporations (including credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial corporations subject to NFRD, households (with sub-categories: mortgages collateralised by residential property, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local government financing, and collateral obtained.
  - Additional splits by lending type: specialised lending, transitional (for CCM), enabling activities, and for CCA: specialised lending, adaptation, enabling.
  - Headline pattern: overall eligibility is roughly stable around 49–52% across dates, with environmentally sustainable shares around 9–11% at the aggregate level; households are consistently shown as 100% eligible with circa 20–22% environmentally sustainable shares, and mortgages mirror this; building renovation loans are shown as fully eligible/sustainable within households.

- GAR KPIs on flows:
  - For 31 Dec 2023 and 30 Jun 2024, flow fields are intentionally left blank; flow reporting starts in Q4 2024 to align with the Integrated Annual Report 2024 approach.
  - As of 31 Dec 2024, flow KPIs show high coverage of new assets (generally around mid-90s to 100%), with environmentally sustainable shares around the low-20s overall; household flows show high coverage and circa 24% sustainable; non-financial corporates and financial corporates present segment-specific coverage and sustainable shares; enabling, transitional/adaptation, and specialised lending splits are provided.

- Methodological and scope notes:
  - Alignment challenge between FINREP and EU Taxonomy: exposures towards non-NFRD financial corporations are placed in “other assets” in the P3 template to reconcile with EU Taxonomy disclosures; totals for “Other financial corporations” account for entities considered financial in FINREP but non-financial under the EU Taxonomy.
  - Household methodology: CCM eligibility is used as the primary measure to capture the full household-related eligibility scope (also covering CCA and Circular Economy) and to avoid double counting.
  - Regulatory update impact: in 2024, household loans collateralised by residential property and renovation loans are included under CCA, reflecting the EU Taxonomy update expanding these products beyond CCM to CCA.

- ESG10 – Other climate change mitigating actions not covered by the EU Taxonomy:
  - Presents exposures that support climate mitigation but do not meet the EU Taxonomy’s strict technical screening criteria or scope.
  - Based on ABN AMRO’s Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS), aligned with market practice and SFDR; a climate-focused subset of SAS-labelled “acceleration” loans is reported (e.g., clean transportation, sustainable real estate).
  - Exposures increased by year-end 2024 versus mid-2024, mainly due to new mortgage production.
  - Notes that only a limited portion of exposures are EU Taxonomy-aligned given its narrow scope and strict criteria; hence, most climate-mitigating exposures appear in this non-Taxonomy template.

scope of eligibility related to households, effectively capturing activities that are also eligible under Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) and Circular Economy (CE). This 
approach ensures a more precise depiction of eligibility and avoids double counting. 
3. The household product loans collateralised by rip and renovation loans have been included in this year's assessment for Climate Change Adaptation, these were previously 
not in scope for this environmental objective. This change aligns with the recent update to the EU Taxonomy regulation, which has expanded the scope of these household

heading: 7.16 ESG10 - Other climate change mitigating actions not covered in the EU Taxonomy
start_phrase: This template includes other climate change mitigating actions that are not aligned with the strict criteria of the EU Taxonomy, but nevertheless support counterparties in mitigating climate change related risks.
summary:
- Purpose and scope: Presents ESG10 exposures—other climate change–mitigating actions not meeting the strict EU Taxonomy criteria but supporting clients in managing climate-related risks. The bank uses a subset of its internal Sustainability Acceleration Standard (SAS), aligned with EU SFDR and market practice, filtered to climate-focused categories (e.g., clean transport, sustainable real estate).
- EU Taxonomy alignment: Only a limited share is EU Taxonomy–aligned due to the Technical Screening Criteria, limited scope (including NFRD), and other strict requirements; therefore, most exposures are reported in this Pillar 3 ESG10 template.
- Risk coverage: Actions primarily mitigate climate transition risk. Physical risk mitigation is flagged mainly for green bonds; loans are reported as mitigating transition risk, not physical risk.
- Instruments and counterparties:
  - Bonds: Green bonds from European banks and sovereigns/government-guaranteed issuers (Austria, Germany, Finland, France, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Philippines, Sweden, EU; Denmark noted in 2023). Use-of-proceeds frameworks cover both mitigation and adaptation.
  - Loans: Financing internally classified as sustainable under SAS with a climate mitigation purpose. Counterparties include financial corporations, non-financial corporations (with a material share collateralised by commercial real estate), and households (predominantly residential mortgages; no separate building renovation loans reported).
- Reported balances (gross carrying amounts, in millions) at 31 Dec 2024:
  - Bonds: Financial corporations ~439; Other counterparties (sovereign/guaranteed) ~1,910.
  - Loans: Financial corporations ~1,665; Non-financial corporations ~14,329 (of which commercial real estate ~5,317); Households ~16,508 (of which residential mortgages ~15,278).
- Time-series context (31 Dec 2023, 30 Jun 2024, 31 Dec 2024): Balances are shown for three dates, with category-level movements over time. The narrative notes higher exposures at 31 Dec 2024 versus 30 Jun 2024, driven mainly by inflows from new mortgage production. Financial- and non-financial-corporate sustainable loans generally trend up across the period; sovereign/guaranteed green bond holdings fluctuate; building renovation loans remain unreported.
- Standards note: Instruments include green, sustainable, and sustainability-linked types under standards other than EU standards.
text:
Other climate change mitigating actions not covered in the EU Taxonomy
This template includes other climate change mitigating actions that are not aligned with the strict criteria of the EU 
Taxonomy, but nevertheless support counterparties in mitigating climate change related risks. 
As a reference, we used the loans that we internally label as ‘acceleration’ based on our Sustainability Acceleration 
Standard (SAS). Our SAS definition is based on current market practice for loans and investments, and is aligned with 
the definitions set in the EU SFDR regulation for client assets. The criteria in the SAS do not only relate to climate 
change, but can also relate to other environmental objectives or social objectives. As this template only focuses on 
climate, we have made a sub-selection of our SAS-aligned loans that specifically relate to climate change based on 
sub-categories in the standard. An example would be an acceleration finance loan used for clean transportation or 
sustainable real estate.
The exposures reported as at 31 December 2024 increased compared to 30 June 2024, mainly as a result of inflow
stemming from new mortgage production (households loans).
We note that, considering the EU Taxonomy, a limited part of our exposures is aligned. This is mainly due to the limited 
scope and strict requirements of the EU Taxonomy as a result of the Technical Screening Criteria and the NFRD scope, 
among others. Therefore, the majority of exposures continue to be reported in this Pillar 3 template.ABN AMRO Pillar 3 Report 2024 ≡
